Reading those referrals preserves the distinction between an incorrect input, a missing warning output and an alarm that does not arm.

topics.title: Removing and Installing a Front Seat
topics.summary: A front seat supports the occupant through its frame, adjustment tracks and body attachments. Removing the assembly also involves electrical connections and the supplemental restraint system (SRS), so installation is more than simply replacing its bolts.

sections.title: The mounting joints carry occupant loads
sections.body: The seat frame and tracks transfer loads into the vehicle body through their mounting points. Material trapped between those joints can prevent the parts from seating as intended. This explains the procedure's emphasis on clear mating surfaces and its prohibition on placing objects within the seat's structural joints.

sections.title: Positioning and electrical preparation create access
sections.body: The seat must be positioned so its mounting bolts are accessible. If a powered track cannot provide that movement, the procedure directs attention to the horizontal motor concern. The specified restraint depowering and harness separation address the electrical connections before the complete seat assembly is lifted away.

sections.title: Installation has a defined fastening sequence
sections.body: The illustrated seat is the driver seat in a left-hand-drive vehicle, with the other seats described as similar. Installation includes a specified bolt order and restraint repowering, so the general instruction to reverse removal has additional requirements. The sequence and fastening values belong to the detailed procedure.

topics.title: Front Seat Track Replacement
topics.summary: The front seat track supports the seat and provides the mechanism for its adjustable position. Replacing it involves transferring the seat’s surrounding components and, for a new driver memory track, establishing the electronic travel limits.

sections.title: Structure and movement share one assembly
sections.body: The track carries the occupant’s weight while allowing the seat to change position. On power seats, motors and mechanical drives produce those adjustments. The memory system also follows position information, allowing it to return to a stored setting and stop movement at the intended limits.

sections.title: Why the cushion and backrest are involved
sections.body: The procedure separates the backrest and the cushion cover-and-foam assembly to make the track available for replacement. On a passenger seat equipped with an original-equipment Occupant Classification System (OCS), that system has its own removal reference. This condition matters because occupant sensing is part of the restraint system, not merely seat adjustment.

sections.title: Understanding the memory-track completion step
sections.body: For a new driver memory seat track, the specified full-travel operation establishes soft stops. These are learned stopping positions used by the control system; incorrect limits can make the seat stop before reaching its available travel. That instruction is conditional and should not be generalized to every seat-track installation.

topics.title: Driver Memory Seat Module
topics.summary: The driver front seat module (DSM) controls the driver’s power seat on vehicles with memory seating. It uses switch requests and position information to move the seat and recall stored positions.

sections.title: Position feedback makes memory movement possible
sections.body: The seat switch sends a request to the DSM, which supplies the appropriate motor circuit. Position sensors tell the module how the seat is moving and where it is. That feedback lets it recall a stored position and recognize when expected movement has stopped during a memory operation.

sections.title: Why replacement begins before removal
sections.body: For a new module, programmable module installation (PMI) begins with the existing DSM still installed. This preserves access to its configuration information before it is disconnected. If the old module cannot communicate, the scan tool may request factory configuration information, called As-Built Data, to support the replacement process.

sections.title: Understanding access position and soft stops
sections.body: The specified seat position creates access for module removal. After replacement, full seat travel establishes the soft stops that govern where movement ends, reducing premature stopping. These replacement-specific instructions are distinct from ordinary removal and refitting, and the reference notes similar work for left-hand-drive and right-hand-drive driver seats.

topics.title: Understanding front-seat electrical features
topics.summary: The front-seat systems adjust seating position and, when equipped, provide heating and cooling. This overview distinguishes direct motor control, driver-seat memory and the separate climate-controlled seat equipment.

sections.title: Memory changes who controls the motors
sections.body: On the non-memory driver seat and powered passenger seat, the switch directly changes motor voltage polarity to select movement direction. With driver memory, the switch instead sends requests to the Driver Seat Module (DSM). That module drives the motors and uses position feedback to record and recall seat settings.

sections.title: Seat climate uses its own hardware
sections.body: Climate-controlled seats have blower assemblies in the cushions and backrests, together with temperature feedback and air-distribution passages. Their fans move conditioned air through the seat structure. The overview separates these comfort components from the positioning motors because a temperature concern and an adjustment concern involve different equipment and control paths.

sections.title: Equipment and operating mode guide interpretation
sections.body: Match the reference to memory, non-memory and climate-seat equipment before following its service information. Motor service boundaries differ: some belong to larger assemblies. With applicable remote-start preferences, outside temperature can trigger seat heating or cooling automatically, and normal adjustment resumes after ignition activation; that temporary behavior differs from ordinary occupied driving.

topics.title: Power, Memory and Climate-Controlled Seats
topics.summary: Front-seat systems use motors to adjust position and, where equipped, separate equipment to heat or cool the seating surfaces. Memory adds position feedback so the driver seat can return to stored settings.

sections.title: Motor direction follows electrical polarity
sections.body: Reversing the electrical polarity supplied to a seat motor reverses its movement. Without memory, the seat switch directly controls the relevant motor circuits. With memory, the driver seat module (DSM) handles motor operation and monitors position sensors, allowing it to recognize and return to a saved seat position.

sections.title: Feedback supports recall and travel limits
sections.body: Position feedback allows memory recall and programmed stopping points before the mechanism reaches its physical limits. If feedback is lost, the affected memory-seat motor can enter limited jog operation. Ignition and gear-position messages also support automatic functions, explaining why seat behavior can depend on information from other vehicle systems.

sections.title: Keep climate control separate from adjustment
sections.body: Optional climate-controlled seats use blower assemblies, thermoelectric devices and temperature sensors in the cushion and backrest. Their control system operates independently of the cabin climate system. Read the memory-seat and seat-climate diagrams separately: one describes positioning and feedback, while the other describes heating, cooling, airflow and settings messages.

topics.title: Front seat electrical diagnosis
topics.summary: Powered front seats combine adjustment motors with optional memory and climate-control equipment. This diagnostic reference separates movement, position feedback, communication and heating or cooling concerns according to the fitted system.

sections.title: Movement and comfort use different hardware
sections.body: Adjustment motors move the seat, while position sensors let a memory system track that movement. Climate-controlled seats use blower assemblies with thermoelectric devices and temperature feedback. Airflow restrictions can reduce their temperature effect even when electrical commands are present, so seat movement and seat temperature require different diagnostic observations.

sections.title: Match the chart to the equipment
sections.body: The driver door module (DDM) receives memory-switch inputs, the driver seat module (DSM) controls memory-seat movement, and the front seat climate control module (SCME) manages fitted climate-controlled seats. Non-memory power seats use a different control arrangement. Identifying the installed system keeps an unrelated module chart from directing the diagnosis.

sections.title: Interpret codes with the observed behavior
sections.body: A diagnostic trouble code (DTC) reports a detected condition rather than proving a motor or module has failed. The reference distinguishes stalled movement, lost position feedback, supply problems and temperature concerns. Its climate checks compare measured temperature changes and operating mode because a displayed cooling request alone does not establish cooling performance.

topics.title: Front seat backrest removal
topics.summary: The front seat backrest supports the occupant's upper body and connects to the seat's reclining structure. This procedure separates the backrest from the seat while accounting for trim, wiring and the different manual or power-seat arrangements.

sections.title: Structural joints carry occupant loads
sections.body: The backrest frame transfers loads through its attachment to the lower seat structure. Upholstery provides comfort, but the mounting joints establish the assembly's strength and alignment. Foreign material trapped in a structural joint can prevent proper seating of the parts, which explains the procedure's warning about clear mating areas.

sections.title: Trim and wiring surround the attachment
sections.body: The procedure removes the complete front seat before addressing handles, side shields, wiring retainers and cover straps. These parts surround or cross the area needed for backrest removal. Positioning them as directed gives access to the structural fasteners while preserving the intended relationship between the seat's wiring and trim.

sections.title: Choose the branch for the seat fitted
sections.body: Separate instructions address a manual driver seat, power seats and a manual passenger seat because their side-shield retention differs. Blower-snorkel details apply only when equipped. The illustrated left-hand-drive driver seat is representative; the appropriate branch and embedded installation details define how the actual seat is handled.

topics.title: Seat backrest climate blower
topics.summary: The front seat backrest blower assembly moves air through a climate-controlled seat. Its fan, thermoelectric device, and temperature feedback work together to deliver the selected heating or cooling effect through the backrest.

sections.title: Airflow inside the backrest
sections.body: The blower connects to a manifold that distributes air through the backrest cushion. Moving air transfers the heating or cooling effect from the assembly toward the occupant. The temperature sensor provides feedback to the seat controller, while the fan supplies the airflow needed for that heat transfer.

sections.title: Why the trim is involved
sections.body: The blower sits within the seat structure, so the procedure includes moving the cover, straps, wiring, and retaining features to reach it. Some versions have a snorkel. The instructions distinguish those versions because the additional duct changes how surrounding trim and straps are arranged.

sections.title: Reading the illustrations carefully
sections.body: Some views show foam removed only for clarity, which does not make foam removal an implied step. The hook-and-loop caution protects its attachment to the foam. Installation also has a specific tie-strap instruction, so the general direction to reverse removal must be read with that exception.

topics.title: Front seat climate control module
topics.summary: The front seat climate control module (SCME) manages heating and cooling for equipped front seats. This replacement procedure addresses its mounting and connectors, along with the configuration transfer required when a new module is installed.

sections.title: Turning comfort requests into seat conditioning
sections.body: The SCME receives seat-climate requests and controls the cushion and backrest blower assemblies. Those assemblies include a thermoelectric device and temperature feedback. Moving conditioned air through the seat changes the occupant’s thermal comfort, while feedback gives the controller information about the assemblies it is operating.

sections.title: Why replacement includes configuration work
sections.body: The reference requires programmable module installation (PMI) to begin while the existing module remains installed and to finish after replacement. This preserves or establishes the vehicle-specific configuration needed by the new electronics. If the old module cannot communicate, the scan-tool process may request the vehicle’s as-built configuration data.

sections.title: Separating access from replacement-only steps
sections.body: The passenger-seat position specified in the procedure provides access to the module beneath it. Locking wedges retain its electrical connections. The illustrated left-hand-drive passenger seat and the right-hand-drive version follow similar work, while the PMI notes explicitly apply to installing a new component rather than every removal.

topics.title: Front seat adjustment switch
topics.summary: The front seat control switch converts your adjustment choice into electrical control of the seat motors. This procedure explains access through the seat's side trim and removal of the switch itself.

sections.title: Memory equipment changes the control path
sections.body: On the driver seat without memory and the power passenger seat, the switch directly changes motor-circuit polarity to select movement direction. With driver-seat memory, it sends a request to the driver seat module (DSM), which powers the appropriate motor. The same adjustment intention therefore reaches the motors through different electrical arrangements.

sections.title: The side shield provides access
sections.body: The switch is attached to the seat's side shield, so the recline handle, shield retainers and control knob are part of reaching it. The specified lifting, outward and forward movements relate to releasing that trim arrangement. Disconnecting the electrical connector separates the switch wiring from the assembly being removed.

sections.title: Keep the illustrated seat variation in mind
sections.body: The manual illustrates a left-hand-drive driver seat and states that the others are similar. Installation follows the removal sequence in reverse, including the details embedded in removal illustrations. A seat that does not move is not proof of a failed switch; the relevant motor and control arrangement still determine diagnostic interpretation.

topics.title: Front seat-cushion blower replacement
topics.summary: A climate-controlled seat uses a blower assembly to move conditioned air through its cushion. This procedure replaces the cushion blower assembly and addresses the passenger-seat sensing components encountered during access.

sections.title: Airflow within the seat
sections.body: The cushion blower assembly combines a fan, a thermoelectric device and temperature feedback. Air movement carries the heating or cooling effect through the seat's distribution structure. This assembly serves the seat itself; the dashboard ventilation blower moves cabin air through a different system and follows a different service procedure.

sections.title: Why cushion construction affects access
sections.body: Access involves the seat trim, cushion cover and foam because those pieces surround the blower assembly. On the passenger side, the Occupant Classification System, or OCS, may be attached to the foam as part of a service assembly. Keeping those calibrated parts together preserves the relationship used to interpret seat loading.

sections.title: Understanding the passenger-seat follow-through
sections.body: The passenger-seat instructions require completed assembly before the OCS reset establishes the unloaded reference. Specified environmental and electrical conditions make that reset meaningful. The subsequent Supplemental Restraint System verification checks the safety system affected by the seat work, explaining why this comfort-component repair includes restraint-related completion requirements.

topics.title: Front seat cushion cover and occupant sensing
topics.summary: The front seat cushion cover secures the upholstery over the cushion foam and support structure. On the passenger seat, its removal also involves occupant-classification equipment, making the correct seat and sensor configuration central to this repair.

sections.title: The cover works with the cushion beneath it
sections.body: Clips and fabric attachment strips hold the cover against the foam, shaping the seating surface. The passenger occupant classification system (OCS) uses information associated with seat loading for restraint decisions. Disturbing the cushion can therefore involve both upholstery attachments and sensing components beneath the occupant.

sections.title: Why the procedure has several branches
sections.body: Manual and power seats have different handles and side-shield arrangements. Passenger seats also differ between original equipment and an installed OCS service kit. With the service kit, the sensing assembly is adhered to the foam, so the prescribed assembly handling protects components that must remain together as calibrated.

sections.title: Reassembly establishes the sensing baseline
sections.body: The passenger-seat reset requires the seat and attached components to be completely assembled and installed because their weight affects the baseline. The procedure then verifies the supplemental restraint system (SRS). Its sequence matters: upholstery attachment, sensor-hose routing and final restraint verification are connected parts of completing this job.

topics.title: Front seat power lumbar assembly
topics.summary: The power lumbar assembly changes the support felt against the occupant's lower back. It is mounted within the front seat backrest and serviced as an assembly.

sections.title: Adjustment changes the backrest support
sections.body: An electrically driven lumbar mechanism changes the support behind the backrest padding. The occupant feels that change through the foam and upholstery rather than contacting the mechanism directly. The seat overview identifies a lumbar motor within the power lumbar assembly, separating this function from the motors that move the seat track.

sections.title: Access passes through the backrest layers
sections.body: The removal sequence moves the cover, straps and retainers to expose the assembly and its J-hook attachments. Climate-controlled seat equipment introduces additional blower-related steps where fitted. Careful release of the hook-and-loop strips matters because pulling them away with the cover can tear their attachment from the foam.

sections.title: Follow trim and airbag details together
sections.body: The procedure passes through the side-airbag deployment-chute area, so trim access and restraint-system condition are connected parts of the job. Installation calls for inspection of the airbag, cavity, mounting surface and chute. The illustrated blower snorkel and driver-seat example provide context, while conditional notes identify equipment-dependent steps.

topics.title: Front head-restraint guide sleeves
topics.summary: Head-restraint guide sleeves fit into the seat backrest and guide the head-restraint posts. They support smooth adjustment and help retain the restraint in its intended position.

sections.title: Guiding and retaining the posts
sections.body: The metal head-restraint posts slide through the sleeves as the restraint is adjusted. The sleeves keep those posts aligned with the seat structure, while the locking features control release and retention. A sleeve that is damaged or incorrectly positioned can interfere with movement even when the head restraint itself looks undamaged.

sections.title: Why the sleeves are replaced
sections.body: This procedure treats removed guide sleeves as discard items and requires new ones during installation. It also warns that the sleeves are not interchangeable between positions. Their outward similarity does not establish identical function, so correct placement is part of restoring both adjustment and retention.

sections.title: Understanding the simplified illustration
sections.body: The reference uses a typical sleeve illustration and shows the backrest cushion removed for clarity. That drawing exposes the retention details; it is not itself an instruction to remove the cushion. Read the locking-tab and sleeve-position details together with the written removal and installation sequence.

topics.title: The Recaro backrest cover
topics.summary: The Recaro front-seat backrest cover is shaped upholstery secured to the seat's foam and supporting structure. On seats with a side airbag, the cover and deployment arrangement also form part of the airbag's intended exit path.

sections.title: Hidden attachments hold the seat's shape
sections.body: Hooks, clips and hook-and-loop strips pull the cover into the backrest contours and keep it located against the foam. Pass-through bezels and the release-handle bezel finish the openings around other seat features. Pulling against an attachment that remains engaged can tear its mounting strip or hook from the foam pad.

sections.title: Why an airbag-equipped cover is replaced
sections.body: The source prohibits repairing backrest covers on seats equipped with side airbags, while allowing cleaning. A repair could change how the cover opens during deployment. The airbag cavity and deployment chute also need their intended shape and freedom from foreign material so the airbag can follow its designed path.

sections.title: Following the Recaro seat branches
sections.body: The procedure covers both Recaro and GT350 Recaro seats, with separate portions identifying their cover-release details. The illustrated driver-seat example is described as similar for the other applicable seats. Seat removal and side-airbag service have their own referenced procedures, while this page explains the upholstery attachments and backrest-cover replacement.

topics.title: 3.7L manual transmission removal
topics.summary: The MT82 manual transmission carries engine torque through selectable gear ratios to the driveline. This removal procedure covers the transmission fitted to the 3.7L Duratec and its connections to the clutch, controls, and supporting structure.

sections.title: Gears, synchronizers, and the clutch
sections.body: The clutch connects engine rotation to the transmission input shaft. Inside the transmission, synchronizers help match rotating speeds before the selected gear is locked into the power path. Moving the gear lever operates the selector mechanism, while clutch release allows that selection to occur without continuous engine torque.

sections.title: Why removal involves several systems
sections.body: The procedure addresses the gearshift mechanism, rear support, starter, wiring, and clutch hydraulic connection because each interfaces with the transmission assembly. The transmission jack and safety strap maintain control of its weight as its vehicle supports are released and the assembly is separated from the engine.

sections.title: Understanding separation and conditional steps
sections.body: The rearward movement described after bellhousing release withdraws the input shaft from the clutch before lowering the transmission. The fluid-draining instruction is conditional on transmission disassembly being required. These details distinguish removing the complete assembly from opening its case, and they should remain tied to this engine-specific procedure.

topics.title: Removing the 5.0L Manual Transmission
topics.summary: The MT82 manual transmission changes the speed and torque delivered from the 5.0L engine toward the rear wheels. This removal procedure separates the transmission from its supporting structure, controls and clutch connection.

sections.title: The clutch joins engine and gearbox
sections.body: The transmission input shaft receives engine torque through the clutch. Inside the gearbox, selected gear combinations determine the relationship between input and output speed. Removing the transmission therefore requires disengaging its input shaft from the clutch, as well as freeing the external connections that keep the assembly attached to the vehicle.

sections.title: Support replaces the normal mounting structure
sections.body: The procedure specifies transmission support before work on the gearshift lever and removal of the rear support structure. Once the crossmember and mounting connections are released, the transmission's weight needs another controlled support path. The specified safety strap keeps the assembly secured during separation and lowering.

sections.title: Read access work and conditional work differently
sections.body: Starter, exhaust and sensor-related steps provide the access and clearance required by this 5.0L procedure. Wiring and the clutch hydraulic connection are also addressed before separation. The fluid-draining note is conditional on planned transmission disassembly, so it should be understood in that context rather than as a general maintenance instruction.

topics.title: Installing the 3.7L MT82 Transmission
topics.summary: The MT82 manual transmission transfers engine power through driver-selected gear ratios. This 3.7L procedure excerpt covers installation connections, structural support and restoration of transmission lubrication and clutch hydraulics.

sections.title: The clutch joins engine and gearbox
sections.body: The input shaft receives drive through the clutch, and the gearbox's synchronized mechanisms select the working gear ratio. Its splined connection must allow the intended clutch relationship, while the pilot-bearing surface supports the input end. The specified preparation addresses those contact surfaces before the transmission is secured.

sections.title: Mounting and connections have distinct jobs
sections.body: Bellhousing fasteners secure the transmission to the engine, while the crossmember and support insulator support the rear assembly and limit vibration transfer. The excerpt also restores the starter, gearshift mechanism, wiring and clutch tube. Each connection returns a different mechanical, electrical or hydraulic function after installation.

sections.title: Two fluid systems need separate attention
sections.body: Transmission filling restores lubrication inside the gearbox. Filling and bleeding the clutch hydraulic system restores the fluid column that transfers pedal movement to clutch release, since trapped air compresses. These are separate references in the installation sequence, and this page's applicability remains the MT82 paired with the 3.7L engine.

topics.title: Installing the 5.0L manual transmission
topics.summary: The MT82 manual transmission provides selectable gear ratios between the 5.0L engine and the driveline. This installation reference restores its mechanical attachment, controls, electrical connections and fluid systems after transmission work.

sections.title: Gears change the relationship between speed and torque
sections.body: The clutch transfers engine rotation to the transmission input shaft. Inside the gearbox, synchronizers bring rotating parts toward matching speeds before a selected gear is engaged. The selected ratio then determines how input rotation reaches the output, allowing different combinations of road speed and driving torque.

sections.title: The gearbox connects several systems
sections.body: Installation includes the bellhousing attachment, transmission support and gearshift lever, along with the clutch hydraulic connection and electrical harnesses. The listed starter and exhaust-related components also belong to this installation sequence. Correct support holds the assembly in position, while restored controls let the driver select gears and release the clutch.

sections.title: Understand lubrication and hydraulic completion
sections.body: The specified small grease application concerns the input-shaft splines and pilot-bearing surface, not the clutch friction faces. Transmission filling supplies internal lubrication, while clutch-system bleeding removes air that would compress instead of transmitting pedal movement effectively. The supplied excerpt is an installation sequence, with separate references carrying those supporting procedures.

topics.title: Convertible trunk lock cylinder
topics.summary: The convertible’s luggage-compartment lock cylinder provides a key-operated mechanical connection to the lid latch. This procedure removes the cylinder and its retaining hardware while separating the latch cable attached to it.

sections.title: From key rotation to latch movement
sections.body: A lock cylinder accepts the matching key and permits its internal mechanism to turn. That movement acts through the connected cable to operate the luggage-compartment latch. The cylinder is therefore the keyed input, while the latch is the separate mechanism that physically retains the lid.

sections.title: Why cable and retainers are involved
sections.body: The cylinder must remain firmly mounted while transferring movement into the cable. Retaining tabs and a clip secure the assembly, while the cable couples it to the latch. The removal sequence separates those relationships so the cylinder can be serviced without treating the entire release mechanism as one part.

sections.title: Following the convertible-specific access
sections.body: The reference begins with rear-seat backrest removal and then addresses the cable, tabs, and retaining clip. Those details describe the convertible arrangement and should not be generalized to a coupe. Installation reverses the sequence, restoring both the cylinder’s retention and its mechanical connection to the latch.

topics.title: Exterior Trunk Release Switch
topics.summary: The luggage compartment lid release switch sends an electrical request to release the trunk latch. This procedure covers the exterior switch retained in the bumper cover and its wiring connection.

sections.title: A button request leads to latch operation
sections.body: Pressing the switch changes an electrical input that the entry system can interpret as a release request. The latch is the mechanism that actually retains and releases the lid. Understanding those separate roles explains why a button that does not produce an opening does not automatically identify a defective switch.

sections.title: The repair concerns the switch assembly
sections.body: The supplied procedure releases the switch from the bumper cover and separates its electrical connector. It does not describe removing the trunk latch or adjusting the lid. Its purpose is to exchange the exterior request device while identifying the two interfaces involved: its mounting retention and its wiring.

sections.title: Keep the switch and system behavior in context
sections.body: The related entry-system overview includes electrically requested luggage-compartment release. The switch page itself supplies only removal and installation information, so it does not establish every condition under which release is allowed. Its illustration is most useful for recognizing the correct exterior switch and how it is retained.

topics.title: How Door Locks and Passive Entry Work
topics.summary: The entry system combines mechanical latches with electrically operated locks and driver-request inputs. It lets the doors lock or unlock through switches, remote keyless entry (RKE) or passive entry, and supports luggage-compartment release.

sections.title: A latch holds the door; a lock controls access
sections.body: The latch mechanically secures the closed door. Its lock actuator changes whether the opening mechanism can release that latch. Reversing electrical polarity across a lock motor reverses its action, allowing the same mechanism to lock or unlock in response to the body control module (BCM).

sections.title: Different requests reach the same locking system
sections.body: Door switches, remote transmitters and passive-entry sensing provide different ways to request access. The driver’s mechanical key provides another locking method. On vehicles with memory seats, door modules relay switch requests; without memory seats, the BCM monitors those switch inputs directly, so the electrical route depends on equipment.

sections.title: Separating requests from actuator movement
sections.body: The system diagrams distinguish switches and key-detection hardware from lock actuators and feedback signals. That distinction matters because receiving a valid request and physically moving a lock are separate events. Reading the matching memory-seat diagram helps trace where the request originates and which electronics carry it onward.

topics.title: How power locks and passive entry work
topics.summary: The entry system turns switch, remote-key, and passive-entry requests into door-lock or luggage-compartment actions. The body control module (BCM) coordinates those requests with latch operation and status feedback.

sections.title: Making the latch lock or unlock
sections.body: Electric motors within the door latches move the locking mechanisms. The BCM's internal relays change the polarity applied to those motors, producing lock or unlock movement. Separate latch feedback reports the resulting state, which explains why a request and an illuminated lock indicator represent different information.

sections.title: Why memory-seat equipment changes the diagram
sections.body: Without memory seats, the BCM directly monitors door-lock switch requests. With memory seats, the driver door module (DDM) and passenger door module (PDM) read those switches and communicate requests over the Controller Area Network (CAN). The same driver action therefore reaches the lock controller through different electrical arrangements.

sections.title: Understanding antennas and system responses
sections.body: Handle sensors detect a passive-entry request, and antennas participate in communication with the key. The operation tables explain lamp, horn, and indicator responses under specific conditions. They also describe switch inhibition after electronic locking, so a deliberately ignored interior-switch request should be understood before interpreting it as a failure.

topics.title: Understanding Lock and Entry Diagnostics
topics.summary: The entry system combines switches, key antennas, electronic controllers and powered latches to respond to lock and release requests. Its diagnostic charts organize faults by the controller and circuit that reported the condition.

sections.title: A request passes through several parts
sections.body: The body control module (BCM) controls door locking, while the radio transceiver module (RTM) receives remote-key information. On vehicles with memory seats, door modules also relay lock-switch requests. A failed response can therefore involve the request input, communication path, electrical output or latch mechanism.

sections.title: Codes separate different kinds of trouble
sections.body: A diagnostic trouble code (DTC) describes an observed condition, such as an open circuit, an unwanted connection to ground or a missing network message. These conditions require different reasoning. An antenna code, for example, identifies an electrical concern without proving that the antenna itself needs replacement.

sections.title: Match the reporting module and symptom
sections.body: Read each chart under its named module, then follow the matching description and diagnostic destination. Some entries also distinguish an indicator that stays on from one that never lights. Remote-start shutdown entries involve powertrain information, so their prescribed diagnostic order matters even though they appear in this entry-system section.

topics.title: Lubricating a door latch
topics.summary: The door latch captures the striker to hold the door closed and releases when the handle operates its mechanism. Lubrication reduces friction within that moving mechanism while preserving the latch’s electrical locking components.

sections.title: Moving surfaces inside the latch
sections.body: As the door closes, the striker turns the latch mechanism into its retained position. Opening the door releases that retention so the striker can leave. Sliding and pivoting surfaces move during each cycle, and a suitable lubricant reduces friction between those surfaces as they engage and release.

sections.title: Why more grease is not better
sections.body: The procedure places the latch in a defined position so lubricant reaches the intended opening, then cycles the mechanism to distribute it. Excess grease can damage the internal lock motor, according to the reference. The controlled application and removal of surplus therefore have a specific protective purpose.

sections.title: Understanding the handle variations
sections.body: The manual illustrates a typical left-front latch and notes that other doors are similar. Exterior handles may operate mechanically or electronically, so their release arrangements are not universal. The procedure concerns lubrication of the latch mechanism; it does not establish the cause of an electrical release or locking concern.

topics.title: Door lock control switch
topics.summary: The door lock control switch lets you request electrical locking or unlocking from inside the car. This procedure removes the switch from the door trim assembly while preserving its retaining features.

sections.title: A button press becomes a request
sections.body: Pressing the switch changes an electrical signal that the lock system recognizes. Without memory-seat equipment, the body control module (BCM) monitors that request directly. With memory equipment, door modules receive the switch input and send the request onward, after which the BCM commands the lock motors.

sections.title: Access the retaining clips
sections.body: The repair begins with front door trim panel removal and then releases the switch’s retaining clips. These clips hold the switch securely within its trim mounting. Understanding that attachment explains why this job concerns access and retention rather than removal of the latch or the motor that actually moves the lock.

sections.title: Apply the illustrated side correctly
sections.body: The illustration uses a left-hand-drive vehicle and the left-side switch, while the reference states that right-hand-drive and opposite-side work is similar. Installation reverses removal. Similarity of access does not make every vehicle’s electrical control arrangement identical, so related wiring should still match the fitted memory-seat equipment.

topics.title: Door lock cylinder removal
topics.summary: The door lock cylinder accepts the mechanical key and transfers its rotation to the door-lock mechanism. This procedure removes the cylinder and its door-handle cover assembly from the front door.

sections.title: A mechanical entry path
sections.body: Inside the cylinder, the correct key aligns the locking elements so the cylinder can turn. That rotation operates the associated lock mechanism. This gives the driver a mechanical way to operate the lock alongside the vehicle’s electronic locking features, whose switches, antennas and control modules perform different tasks.

sections.title: Retention explains the release sequence
sections.body: The repair accesses a release screw through a grommet opening and removes the cylinder with the handle cover. The specified screw movement extends beyond the point where the handle first releases because the retaining mechanism must also be positioned for installation. Stopping at initial release would miss that installation detail.

sections.title: Use the correct vehicle-side illustration
sections.body: The reference illustrates a left-hand-drive vehicle and states that right-hand-drive work is similar. Its removal notes also contain installation information, so reversing the sequence includes respecting those details. This page describes physical cylinder removal; it does not establish a key-coding procedure or diagnose the electronic door-lock system.

topics.title: Removing the exterior door handle
topics.summary: The exterior front door handle provides the hand-operated connection to the door’s release mechanism and incorporates electrical connections for entry functions. Its removal procedure protects both the handle retention mechanism and the wiring inside the door.

sections.title: The handle has mechanical and electrical jobs
sections.body: Pulling the handle operates the door-release mechanism, while the entry system uses the handle’s antenna and touch-sensor functions to recognize a lock or unlock request. The lock-cylinder cover assembly also forms part of the mounting arrangement. These overlapping functions explain why removing the visible handle involves more than its outer trim.

sections.title: Why the procedure opens the door interior
sections.body: Removing the trim panel and lower watershield provides access to the handle connector from inside the door. That access matters because pulling the handle too far while it remains connected loads the wiring directly. The release screw frees the retaining mechanism, but the specified full movement also prepares it for reinstallation.

sections.title: Understanding release and re-engagement
sections.body: The handle can appear released or engaged before the screw has completed its prescribed travel. The installation instructions account for that difference and describe how light pressure accompanies re-engagement. The illustrations show the left side and left-hand-drive arrangement; the source identifies the opposite side and right-hand-drive procedure as similar.

topics.title: Exterior door handle reinforcement
topics.summary: The exterior front door handle reinforcement supports the handle’s mounting within the door. This repair reference addresses the reinforcement in conjunction with front door latch removal and identifies a step that applies when installing a new component.

sections.title: Supporting the force of a handle pull
sections.body: An exterior handle must remain supported while the user pulls it to operate the door-opening mechanism. A reinforcement provides a stable mounting structure and distributes those operating forces into the door assembly. Its mechanical support role is separate from the electrical functions associated with locking and passive entry.

sections.title: Why the latch procedure is referenced
sections.body: The supplied sequence begins with removal of the front door latch, placing reinforcement service within a larger access operation. It then marks the reinforcement step as necessary when installing a new component. That conditional note matters because it distinguishes replacement-related work from every possible reason for opening the door assembly.

sections.title: Using the brief procedure accurately
sections.body: The left-hand side is illustrated and the right-hand side is described as similar. Installation reverses the removal sequence. Because the text is brief, the illustrations and referenced latch procedure carry the attachment and access details; the component name alone does not establish fastener locations or a separate adjustment procedure.

topics.title: Front door latch and release connections
topics.summary: The front door latch captures the striker to keep the door closed and incorporates functions used by the locking system. This procedure removes the latch while managing its handle linkages, electrical connection and surrounding door hardware.

sections.title: Latching, releasing and locking are related jobs
sections.body: The latch mechanically holds the door shut. Handle cables and linkage transmit a release request, while the locking mechanism controls whether that request can release the door. Electrical lock motors and feedback within the latch connect this mechanical assembly to the vehicle's power-lock system.

sections.title: Window hardware shares the working space
sections.body: The specified access sequence includes the window glass, exterior handle and rear glass run, then positions part of the regulator aside. These components occupy the same door cavity as the latch and its linkages. Their removal or repositioning creates the clearance described by the procedure.

sections.title: Separate basic removal from replacement-only work
sections.body: Several cable, reinforcement and rod operations are marked as necessary only when installing a new component. Those notes distinguish removing the existing assembly from transferring its associated pieces. The left side is illustrated, with the right described as similar; routing and attachment details remain important on either side.

topics.title: Understanding the Hood Latch
topics.summary: The hood latch mechanically holds the hood closed and releases it when the release cable is pulled. Its hood-ajar switch also supplies an electrical indication of whether the hood is closed.

sections.title: Mechanical retention and electrical status
sections.body: The latch captures the hood's mating striker as the hood closes. Pulling the release cable moves the latch mechanism so the hood can be released. The hood-ajar switch reports latch status electrically; its connector serves a different purpose from the cable that physically operates the latch.

sections.title: Why the original position is marked
sections.body: The latch must meet the striker in the correct position. The procedure preserves a reference by marking the latch mounting position before removal. Returning the latch to those marks helps restore its previous alignment, which matters because a shifted latch can change how the hood engages and sits.

sections.title: Follow the connections and alignment stages
sections.body: The radiator sight shield removal provides access to the latch. During installation, the cable and switch connection are restored before the mounting position is finalized. Initial loose fastening allows alignment with the reference marks. The illustrations show a left-hand-drive vehicle, with a similar process for right-hand drive.

topics.title: Hood release cable
topics.summary: The hood release cable carries a pull from the interior handle to the hood latch. Its outer casing and retained route allow that movement to reach the latch instead of being lost through movement of the cable assembly.

sections.title: How the handle releases the latch
sections.body: A flexible inner cable slides inside an outer casing. Pulling the handle draws the inner cable relative to the casing and moves the release mechanism at the latch. The casing’s supports matter because they provide the reaction needed to turn handle travel into useful movement at the other end.

sections.title: Why the job follows the whole route
sections.body: The replacement procedure follows the cable from the interior handle, through the cowl, to the latch area. Trim panels, routing clips, a bracket and a grommet all appear because the cable passes through several supported sections. The grommet also protects the cable where it passes through the body opening.

sections.title: Recognizing conditional access steps
sections.body: Removal of the audio digital signal processing (DSP) module applies only when that equipment is fitted. The left-hand-drive illustration has a similar right-hand-drive procedure. Read the routing illustrations with the attachment steps: they explain how the cable’s supports and passage through the cowl relate to the replacement.

topics.title: Hood Release Handle Replacement
topics.summary: The hood release handle is the driver's mechanical input to the hood-latch release system. This procedure removes the handle from its retained mounting so that the handle itself can be serviced.

sections.title: Hand movement becomes cable movement
sections.body: Pulling a hood release handle provides leverage to move the release cable and operate the latch mechanism. The handle's mounting must resist that pull so movement reaches the cable rather than simply moving the handle assembly. Its retaining features therefore support a working mechanical control, not just an interior trim piece.

sections.title: The access cover exposes retention
sections.body: The repair sequence addresses the handle's access cover and clips before removing the handle. Releasing those clips allows the mounting to separate without relying on force against still-engaged retainers. The procedure's specified release method concerns this attachment, rather than adjustment of the hood latch at the front of the vehicle.

sections.title: Keep this job's scope in view
sections.body: The illustrations show the left-hand-drive arrangement, with right-hand drive described as similar. Installation reverses the removal sequence to restore the handle and cover retention. This short reference covers handle removal; it does not establish that a hood-release concern originates in the handle rather than another part of the release system.

topics.title: Interior front door handle
topics.summary: The interior front door handle provides the occupant's mechanical means of releasing the door latch. This procedure removes the handle assembly and explains when its separate door lock control switch is transferred during replacement.

sections.title: Handle movement operates the latch release
sections.body: Pulling the interior handle transfers movement to the door's latch-release mechanism. The handle mounting supports that repeated load, so the handle needs secure retention as well as free movement. The nearby electrical lock switch serves a separate request function within the door's locking system.

sections.title: The trim panel provides access to the mounting
sections.body: The procedure begins with removal of the front door trim panel so the handle's attachment can be reached. A nut and retaining clips secure the handle assembly. Releasing the intended retainers allows removal without relying on force against the surrounding trim or mounting features.

sections.title: Read side and replacement notes carefully
sections.body: The illustrations show the left side of a left-hand-drive vehicle, with the other configurations described as similar. The lock-switch removal step applies only when installing a new handle component. That note explains why switch transfer belongs to replacement work rather than every instance of handle removal.

topics.title: Rear keyless-entry antenna replacement
topics.summary: The rear keyless-entry antenna supports passive-key detection around the luggage compartment. This procedure explains access to the antenna and its electrical connection for removal and installation on coupe and convertible applications.

sections.title: How the rear antenna participates
sections.body: The body control module activates the rear antenna to transmit a low-frequency signal that wakes a passive key. The key’s reply is received elsewhere by the radio transceiver module. This division matters because the rear antenna supplies part of the communication process rather than independently deciding whether the luggage lid may release.

sections.title: Why the trim appears in the procedure
sections.body: The luggage compartment scuff plate and its retainers are part of the access sequence. Once access is available, the procedure addresses the antenna connector and mounting retainers. Those steps separate the electrical connection from the physical attachment, allowing the antenna to be removed without treating surrounding trim as part of the antenna.

sections.title: Reading the body-style notes
sections.body: The coupe is illustrated, with the convertible described as similar. The luggage lid is also omitted from an illustration for clarity; that does not add lid removal to the procedure. Installation reverses the documented removal sequence, and this page does not introduce a separate antenna programming requirement.

topics.title: Coupe trunk latch replacement
topics.summary: The coupe’s luggage-compartment lid latch holds the trunk lid closed and releases it when operated. This procedure removes the latch while accounting for its emergency-release handle, trim, electrical connection, and mounting hardware.

sections.title: Retaining and releasing the lid
sections.body: The latch captures a striker as the lid closes, mechanically resisting the lid’s tendency to open. Releasing the latch frees the striker so the lid can rise. The emergency handle provides an interior release, while the electrical connection supports the latch’s place in the vehicle’s release system.

sections.title: Why the handle and trim come first
sections.body: The emergency handle, latch cover, and lid trim overlap the latch’s service access. Their tabs and retainers hold those pieces in place without being the latch’s main mounting hardware. Separating them in sequence exposes the assembly and avoids forcing a cover against a tab that still retains it.

sections.title: Separating attachments by their purpose
sections.body: The procedure distinguishes handle retention, cover retention, trim fasteners, wiring, and latch mounting nuts. Each serves a different relationship within the assembly. Installation reverses removal to restore those relationships. This reference applies to the coupe lid latch and should not be substituted for the convertible lock-cylinder procedure.

topics.title: Convertible rear quarter window glass
topics.summary: The convertible's rear quarter window is the movable side glass behind the door opening. Its regulator raises and lowers the glass, while its installed alignment helps it meet the surrounding seals and adjoining glass.

sections.title: The regulator carries the glass
sections.body: The glass is attached to a regulator assembly driven by an electric motor. The regulator guides its travel rather than leaving the glass free to move within the body opening. The convertible's master window switch controls these rear quarter windows, and the system description also relates window opening to convertible-top operation.

sections.title: Position determines access to the attachments
sections.body: The procedure removes the glass and regulator assembly together, with separation required when installing new glass. It specifies the fully raised position because that position exposes the attachment access needed for separation. An inoperative window therefore changes the access sequence described in the reference, rather than proving that the glass itself needs replacement.

sections.title: Distinguish side-specific access and final adjustment
sections.body: Right-side access includes the radio transceiver module (RTM), while the other main steps apply to both sides. The note about the convertible top being removed explains illustration visibility. Installation ends with a separate glass-adjustment procedure because reinstalling the assembly's fasteners alone does not establish its final alignment against the seals.

topics.title: Convertible Rear Quarter Window Regulator
topics.summary: The rear quarter-window regulator supports and moves the convertible’s small rear side glass. Its motor supplies motion, while the regulator mechanism guides the glass through its travel and holds it in position.

sections.title: Motor motion becomes glass travel
sections.body: The motor and regulator work together, but they are separate components in this procedure. The regulator carries the glass and controls its movement relative to the surrounding body and seals. Correct positioning matters because the quarter glass must meet the door glass and convertible-top sealing surfaces.

sections.title: Why access depends on glass position
sections.body: The procedure explains that the glass must reach its fully raised position before it can be separated from the regulator. If it cannot move electrically, the specified motor-removal branch permits repositioning for fastener access. On the right side, removal also involves the radio transceiver module (RTM).

sections.title: Separating illustrations from prerequisites
sections.body: The top assembly is shown removed for clarity, which does not make its removal a stated requirement. Speaker, bracket and watershield steps provide access to the glass-and-regulator assembly. Some separation steps apply only when installing a new component, and the concluding glass adjustment restores its relationship to the adjacent seals.

topics.title: Convertible rear quarter window motor
topics.summary: The rear quarter window motor powers movement of the convertible’s small rear side glass. It drives the regulator mechanism, which supports the glass and translates motor rotation into window travel.

sections.title: The motor supplies motion; the regulator guides it
sections.body: The motor and regulator are related but distinct parts. The motor generates rotation, while the regulator controls how the supported glass rises and lowers. On the convertible, rear quarter windows can be operated from the master window switch, and the window system also supports coordinated lowering for top operation.

sections.title: Motor access begins with the regulator assembly
sections.body: This repair removes the rear quarter window regulator before separating its motor. The right-hand side is illustrated, with the left-hand procedure described as similar. Treating regulator removal as a linked job preserves the access and handling information that is not repeated on the shorter motor page.

sections.title: Adjustment restores the glass relationship
sections.body: Installation includes a separate rear quarter glass adjustment procedure because motor operation alone does not establish correct glass alignment. The glass must meet adjoining surfaces and seals properly. Convertible feature notes also matter: door-window behavior described elsewhere should not be assumed for this rear quarter window.

topics.title: Repairing Rear Window Grid Lines
topics.summary: The heated rear-window grid uses thin conductive lines to turn electrical energy into heat that clears the glass. This repair restores a broken surface conductor, with related instructions also covering antenna lines on the glass.

sections.title: A surface line carries the current
sections.body: The conductive material is bonded to the glass surface rather than buried inside it. A break interrupts the electrical path, so a heater line can stop warming its area of glass. Antenna lines carry radio signals instead of serving the same heating purpose, but their surface construction also makes them vulnerable.

sections.title: Repair thickness affects electrical resistance
sections.body: The repair coating bridges the break and overlaps sound conductor on either side. Too little coating or inadequate drying can leave excessive resistance at the repair, reducing defrost performance and concentrating heat locally. The brown appearance layer and the conductive silver layer have different jobs in restoring the damaged line.

sections.title: Appearance alone does not establish continuity
sections.body: A damaged line may still look complete because residue remains on the glass. That explains the procedure's distinction between visual appearance and electrical diagnosis. Surface preparation, masking, coating and drying each support a continuous, well-bonded repair; the technical procedure supplies the material-specific details and final operating check.

topics.title: Rear-Window Heater Terminal Repair
topics.summary: The rear-window heater lead terminal connects the vehicle wiring to the conductive heating grid on the glass. This repair restores that electrical attachment to sound bus-bar material so current can reach the grid and warm the window.

sections.title: How the grid clears the glass
sections.body: Electrical current passing through the rear-window grid produces heat, which helps clear condensation and frost. The bus bar distributes current between the lead connection and the grid lines. A detached terminal interrupts that connection, so an intact-looking grid may still lack the electrical path needed to heat.

sections.title: Why clean conductive material matters
sections.body: The replacement terminal must contact sound conductive material rather than a damaged patch where the original attachment has pulled away. Cleaning removes contamination that would interfere with the soldered joint. Placement therefore depends on the usable bus-bar surface and available space, not simply on covering the old terminal outline.

sections.title: Understanding heating and cooling cues
sections.body: The terminal’s pre-applied solder and temperature-sensitive paint make the specified heat application observable. Holding it steady while the joint cools prevents movement before the solder solidifies. The manual’s heat-source restrictions protect surrounding materials, and its final operating check confirms that the repaired connection actually delivers current to the heater grid.

topics.title: Front door window switch replacement
topics.summary: The front door window control switch turns a finger movement into a request to raise or lower the glass. This procedure explains how the switch and its surrounding bezel are separated for replacement.

sections.title: The switch starts the movement
sections.body: The window switch requests a direction; the motor and regulator produce the actual glass movement. The driver’s master switch can control both door windows, while the passenger switch controls its own window. On a convertible, the master control also provides operation of the rear quarter windows.

sections.title: Why switch and bezel are distinguished
sections.body: The bezel is the surrounding trim that retains the switch assembly in the door. The procedure first addresses that assembly and its electrical connector, then distinguishes driver-side retainers from the passenger-side retaining tab. Separating the switch from the bezel is specifically associated with installing a new component.

sections.title: Matching side and window features
sections.body: The illustrations use one steering and door-side arrangement while noting that the others are similar. Expected switch behavior still depends on equipment: convertibles lack one-touch up and bounce-back. The removal reference describes physical replacement; the operating overview explains which glass movements a particular switch command should request.

topics.title: Front Door Window Glass
topics.summary: The front door glass moves within guides and attaches to the mechanism that raises and lowers it. This procedure separates the glass from that mechanism, then restores its alignment and the power-window system’s learned operation.

sections.title: Movement depends on support and alignment
sections.body: The regulator moves the glass, while the guides control its path through the door. At the top of travel, the glass must meet the surrounding seals evenly. If its position changes during replacement, the motor can still move it while the glass fits poorly or encounters unnecessary resistance.

sections.title: Why the surrounding parts are involved
sections.body: The speaker and watershields are included because they affect access inside the door. The glass itself has bolted attachments and retaining clips, so removing fasteners alone does not complete its release. The specified glass position brings the attachment arrangement into the condition used by the illustrated procedure.

sections.title: Adjustment and initialization serve different purposes
sections.body: The final adjustment establishes the glass’s physical fit, with separate references for coupe and convertible. Initialization addresses the power-window control’s learned travel. Those are related but distinct tasks. The overview also notes that convertibles lack one-touch raising and bounce-back, so the coupe’s feature behavior should not be assumed for both body styles.

topics.title: Front door window regulator
topics.summary: The window regulator supports the door glass and guides its movement as the motor raises or lowers it. This procedure replaces the mechanism and restores its alignment with the frameless door glass.

sections.title: Guiding the glass
sections.body: The motor supplies motion, while the regulator translates that motion into controlled glass travel. Its mounting position influences how the glass approaches the weatherstrip. On a frameless door, that relationship matters because the glass must move freely while also meeting the surrounding seals in the intended position.

sections.title: Preserving mounting relationships
sections.body: The procedure removes the glass first and records the regulator mounting positions before releasing the mechanism. Those marks preserve useful alignment information. The described rotations allow the regulator halves to pass through the door opening, while moving the wiring aside prevents it from remaining caught in the removal path.

sections.title: Alignment and initialization
sections.body: Installation includes returning the regulator to its marks, following the appropriate coupe or convertible glass-adjustment reference, and performing window initialization. Mechanical adjustment establishes the glass fit; initialization establishes the system's learned operation. The motor has a separate procedure, with its removal here conditional on installing a new regulator.

topics.title: Front window regulator motor
topics.summary: The front window regulator motor supplies the motion that raises and lowers the door glass. The regulator converts that rotation into controlled glass travel, while adjustment and initialization establish the finished window’s mechanical and electronic operation.

sections.title: Motor motion and glass movement
sections.body: The motor and regulator have different jobs: the motor produces rotation, and the regulator supports and moves the glass. On the Mustang’s frameless door, glass position also matters where the window meets the weatherstrip. Incorrect alignment can interfere with that fit even when the motor runs.

sections.title: Why the job includes adjustment
sections.body: The motor procedure begins with removal of the regulator assembly, then separates the motor from it. After installation, the manual calls for glass adjustment and power-window initialization. Adjustment addresses the glass’s physical position; initialization establishes the electronic operating reference needed by the applicable window system.

sections.title: Matching the body style
sections.body: The illustrated left side also explains the similar right-side job, but glass adjustment has separate coupe and convertible references. Window features differ too: the supplied overview excludes one-touch closing and bounce-back from convertibles. Read the initialization and adjustment references for the actual body style rather than assuming identical behavior.

topics.title: Why fixed-glass bonding matters
topics.summary: Fixed glass is bonded to the body with urethane adhesive instead of moving in a window regulator. This repair renews that bond so the glass remains retained and the opening stays sealed against air and water.

sections.title: The bond depends on its supporting surfaces
sections.body: The urethane joins the glass to the body's pinch-weld flange. Clean, sound surfaces let the adhesive form a dependable connection, while dirt, damaged coatings or corrosion can undermine it. Protecting and restoring the flange matters because corrosion affects both the bonding surface and a structural part of the body.

sections.title: Adhesive timing affects glass retention
sections.body: Cut urethane surfaces lose bonding effectiveness as they remain exposed, and newly applied adhesive has a limited installation window. A continuous bead prevents leak paths. Curing then develops the required retention, which explains the restriction on driving before cure and the provision for open windows to prevent door-closing pressure from disturbing the fresh bond.

sections.title: Glass equipment changes the repair branch
sections.body: This procedure requires replacement of windshields equipped with a camera bracket or adhesive mouldings rather than reuse. Camera-equipped replacement glass also requires the specified locating features for alignment. Read new-glass and reusable-glass preparation separately, and retain the camera-alignment requirement when that equipment is present.

topics.title: Front Door Glass Guides
topics.summary: The front door glass runs and brackets guide the window as it rises and lowers. Their position controls the glass’s path, making their removal and refitting an alignment-sensitive job rather than simply exchanging mounting hardware.

sections.title: Guides establish the window’s path
sections.body: The regulator supplies movement, while the fore and aft glass runs constrain where the glass travels. Fore means toward the front of the door; aft means toward the rear. Their alignment helps the glass move without binding and arrive at the surrounding seals in the intended position.

sections.title: Why the two removal paths differ
sections.body: The fore guide procedure uses access through the speaker opening. The aft guide procedure includes glass removal and moving the Driver Door Module (DDM) aside. The location marks specified for both guides preserve a reference for refitting, because changing the mounting position changes the path the glass follows.

sections.title: Reading the final setup requirements
sections.body: Installation includes glass adjustment and power-window initialization after the guides are restored. Adjustment addresses physical fit; initialization addresses learned window operation. Separate adjustment references apply to coupe and convertible bodies. The left side is illustrated, with a similar procedure for the right, so image orientation should be read in that context.

topics.title: How the message center gets its information
topics.summary: The message center is the information display within the instrument panel cluster (IPC). It turns information from vehicle systems into useful status displays and warnings that explain more than a gauge or warning lamp alone.

sections.title: Many systems contribute to one display
sections.body: Some information arrives through dedicated wires, while other information arrives as network messages from control modules. For example, the body control module requests a low-brake-fluid warning when it detects that condition. The display presents the request; the condition being reported originates elsewhere in the vehicle.

sections.title: Buttons select information and acknowledge warnings
sections.body: The left steering-wheel buttons produce different electrical responses that the steering column control module recognizes. These inputs let the driver navigate the message center. A warning can replace the selected display, and acknowledging it restores access to other information without necessarily correcting the condition that caused it.

sections.title: Match the message to its equipment
sections.body: The network chart identifies each message's source and purpose. Equipment matters: the listed 2.3L, 3.7L and non-Performance Package 5.0L applications use an oil-pressure switch, while the Performance Package 5.0L uses a pressure sensor. Their electrical inputs differ even though both support oil-pressure information.

topics.title: Understanding the Airbag and Pretensioner System
topics.summary: The supplemental restraint system (SRS) combines airbags, seatbelt pretensioners, sensors and an electronic controller. It supplements the seat belts by managing occupant movement when the controller determines that a crash requires deployment.

sections.title: Sensors inform selective deployment
sections.body: The restraints control module (RCM) evaluates impact information alongside occupant-related inputs. Airbags provide cushioning, while pretensioners tighten the belts to reduce slack. Deployment depends on the event and sensor information, so the system does not necessarily activate every available device during the same crash.

sections.title: Body style changes the component map
sections.body: The location views distinguish coupe side curtains and C-pillar impact sensors from convertible upper side airbags. They also identify knee airbags, belt devices and seat sensors. Left-hand-drive and right-hand-drive descriptions change some driver/passenger labels, making the correct view essential before interpreting a component’s identity.

sections.title: Why connector seating affects self-checks
sections.body: Connector position assurance (CPA) tabs secure deployable-component connectors and release their protective shorting bars. An incompletely seated tab can leave the shorting feature active and cause a monitored circuit fault. This explains why dedicated connector-handling and depowering procedures are part of restraint service, even when a connector appears attached.

topics.title: How airbags and pretensioners work together
topics.summary: The supplemental restraint system (SRS) combines airbags, seatbelt pretensioners and electronic sensing to supplement the seatbelts. It selects appropriate deployable restraints when crash information indicates that their protection is needed.

sections.title: Crash inputs guide selective deployment
sections.body: The restraints control module (RCM) continuously evaluates sensor inputs. Airbags cushion occupant movement, while pretensioners tighten the belts during a qualifying event. Deployment depends on crash severity and other inputs, so different devices may activate for different occupants without that difference proving a system fault.

sections.title: Occupant information changes the decision
sections.body: The occupant classification system (OCS) senses pressure in a bladder within the front passenger seat and reports information to the RCM. The controller uses this alongside other inputs when determining passenger restraint deployment. This explains why seat sensing, buckle information and airbag operation appear in one system description.

sections.title: Read body-style branches and warning behavior
sections.body: The diagrams distinguish coupe side curtains from convertible upper side airbags. Their message charts explain information sharing, while the warning-indicator description explains self-checks and communication concerns. These are system relationships, not permission to test deployable circuits directly; the dedicated restraint procedures govern depowering and handling.

topics.title: Centering the clockspring
topics.summary: Clockspring adjustment establishes the centered position of the flexible electrical cable behind the steering wheel. This procedure applies to vehicles without adaptive steering and preserves cable travel in both steering directions.

sections.title: Why the cable needs a center
sections.body: The clockspring's internal ribbon cable winds and unwinds as its rotor turns. It has finite travel, so starting too far toward either end can exhaust that travel before the steering wheel reaches its normal limit. Correct centering prevents the cable from being pulled against its internal attachment.

sections.title: What the adjustment actually establishes
sections.body: This is a mechanical positioning procedure for the clockspring rotor. The reference uses a defined turning sequence and connector orientation to locate the intended center. Its warning about resistance matters because the ribbon cable can act as the stop; forcing rotation can break the connection rather than reveal extra travel.

sections.title: Keeping the established position
sections.body: The final instruction prevents the rotor from moving after centering, with adhesive tape identified for retaining the position. Losing that position would undo the adjustment before installation. The typical illustration explains the concept, while the explicit adaptive-steering exclusion determines whether this particular procedure is applicable.

topics.title: Restoring restraints after deployment
topics.summary: The supplemental restraint system (SRS) coordinates airbags and seatbelt pretensioners to supplement the seatbelts during a collision. This inspection and repair reference explains what must be restored after deployment or a recorded crash event.

sections.title: Deployment depends on the collision
sections.body: The restraints control module (RCM) evaluates crash sensor information and commands the appropriate deployable devices. Airbags cushion occupants, while pretensioners tighten belts to reduce slack. Different combinations may activate in different collisions, so an undeployed airbag beside a deployed pretensioner does not by itself indicate a system failure.

sections.title: Why the inspection extends beyond airbags
sections.body: Deployment uses devices that require replacement, and collision forces can also damage their mounting structures, wiring, seats and belt anchors. The procedure specifies replacement of deployed devices, impact sensors and the RCM under its stated event conditions. Driver-airbag deployment also brings specific steering wheel, clockspring and steering-column replacement requirements.

sections.title: Following each event-specific requirement
sections.body: Read the conditions attached to each repair carefully: pretensioner deployment, occupant classification system damage and stored event information lead to different requirements. A diagnostic trouble code (DTC) records a detected condition. The final checks establish that restraint faults are resolved, while the crash-status reset addresses a separate recorded vehicle state.

topics.title: Understanding restraint device disposal
topics.summary: Pyrotechnic restraint devices use a controlled chemical reaction to inflate airbags or move protective mechanisms such as seatbelt pretensioners. This disposal procedure accounts for devices that can retain an unfired charge after a fault or collision.

sections.title: What the stored charge does
sections.body: The supplemental restraint system (SRS) commands selected devices during a crash. Airbags create a cushion, while pretensioners quickly remove seatbelt slack. Deployment depends on crash conditions, so a device that did not fire is not automatically faulty. It may still contain an active charge.

sections.title: Why disposal follows separate paths
sections.body: Disposal depends on whether a device is undeployed and inoperative, deployed, or requires controlled deployment under the manual’s dedicated procedure. The reference places inoperative airbags, seatbelt pretensioners and inflatable seatbelt inflators on a mandatory return list.
