sections.body: The table distinguishes left, right and rear audio channels, then separate noise-control pairs and the network connection. Positive and negative audio labels identify paired signals rather than ordinary body-ground connections. No operating-power or body-ground feed is identified in this table, so this view does not represent every electrical requirement of the amplifier.

topics.title: Diagnostic Data Link Connection
topics.summary: The data link connector (DLC) is the vehicle’s electrical interface for a diagnostic scan tool. Connector C251 provides protected power, ground paths and communication circuits so the tool can exchange information with vehicle electronics.

sections.title: Power and communication have different jobs
sections.body: The power feed allows a connected diagnostic device to receive vehicle electrical power, while ground provides its return and reference paths. Separate controller area network circuits carry messages. A tool can therefore have power without successfully communicating, because its supply and data connections perform different tasks.

sections.title: Recognizing the network pairs
sections.body: The table identifies high and low conductors for a high-speed network and a second high-speed network. Each pair works together to encode information through the voltage difference between its conductors. The words high and low name the paired data paths; they do not mean ordinary power and ground.

sections.title: Understanding the connector-face reference
sections.body: The face view establishes orientation and separates used positions from unused ones. Several wire details are represented by asterisks, so the page does not supply a complete color guide. Its assignments explain the interface, while the relevant network diagnostic determines what a communication failure means for the connected systems.

topics.title: Glove-Compartment Lamp Connection
topics.summary: The glove-compartment lamp illuminates the storage area so its contents are easier to see. Its connector provides a battery-saver-controlled supply and an instrument-panel ground return.

sections.title: Completing the lamp’s electrical path
sections.body: The lamp produces light when its operating conditions allow current to pass through the light source. The listed supply provides energy, while the ground completes the return path. A break or poor contact on either side can prevent illumination, even when the other side of the connection remains intact.

sections.title: Why the supply mentions battery saving
sections.body: The feed is identified with the battery-saver function, which can switch interior-lighting power off to reduce battery discharge. That description matters when interpreting an unlit lamp: supply availability depends on the controlling system’s state. The connector page itself does not give the timer rules or the lamp’s full switching arrangement.

sections.title: Using the connector information
sections.body: The connector face and wire descriptions distinguish the controlled feed from the instrument-panel ground. The reference also identifies a service pigtail, meaning a repair connector assembly is cataloged. It does not prescribe connector replacement or prove a failed lamp; the applicable lighting procedure supplies the diagnostic context.

topics.title: Passenger Airbag Connection: C256
topics.summary: The passenger airbag cushions the front passenger during a qualifying crash as part of the supplemental restraint system (SRS). Connector C256 carries dedicated deployment circuits for its inflation stages and adaptive venting function.

sections.title: Inflation and venting have separate roles
sections.body: The connector assignments distinguish separate passenger-airbag deployment stages from adaptive venting. Inflation creates the cushion, while venting influences how gas leaves it as the occupant loads the bag. The restraints control module selects appropriate deployment actions using crash and occupant information; every circuit need not activate together.

sections.title: Dedicated circuit pairs carry deployment current
sections.body: Each listed function has its own positive and negative circuit pair. These are controlled restraint circuits, so a negative label should not be interpreted as permission to connect that conductor to vehicle ground. The assignments also distinguish unused positions from connections belonging to a deployment function.

sections.title: Why the connector details matter
sections.body: The face view establishes connector orientation and the identity of each circuit. Restraint connectors also use assurance features that affect their protective shorting bars and monitored resistance. This reference supports identification within the dedicated SRS procedure; it is not a guide to applying power or independently probing deployment circuits.

topics.title: Passenger knee airbag harness junction
topics.summary: C2600 is an inline junction between harness sections 14B242 and 14401 carrying passenger knee airbag circuits and an instrument-panel ground. It preserves separate electrical paths across the harness connection without acting as an electronic controller.

sections.title: The junction serves a deployable restraint branch
sections.body: The passenger knee airbag provides supplemental restraint for the lower-body area during an appropriate deployment. Its paired control circuits pass through this connector on their way between harness sections. A separate ground circuit is identified for the instrument-panel structure, so the junction carries more than the deployment pair.

sections.title: Deployment return and structural ground are distinct
sections.body: The positive and negative airbag labels identify the two sides of the designated deployment circuit. The instrument-panel ground is separately assigned and should remain conceptually separate from that pair. Treating every negative or return label as the same electrical path would erase an important distinction in this restraint connection.

sections.title: Match circuit identifiers across both faces
sections.body: The male and female tables show different wire colors and gauges on opposite harness sides while retaining matching circuit identities. The face drawings establish orientation, and the unused position remains distinct from active paths. Any handling belongs within the prescribed supplemental restraint system procedure, rather than improvised continuity checks.

topics.title: Passenger knee-airbag connection
topics.summary: The passenger knee airbag helps manage lower-body movement during a qualifying crash as part of the supplemental restraint system (SRS). Connector C2607 carries its paired deployment-circuit connections.

sections.title: Deployment is a controlled system decision
sections.body: The restraints control module (RCM) monitors crash-related inputs and determines which restraint devices should deploy. When required, it supplies deployment energy through the appropriate circuit. The knee airbag works as part of that coordinated response, so the presence or absence of its deployment cannot be judged solely from whether another airbag deployed.

sections.title: Connector security affects circuit monitoring
sections.body: Deployable restraint connectors use connector position assurance (CPA) features to secure the connection and manage protective shorting features. The system can detect a fault when a connector appears attached but its assurance feature is not fully seated. This explains why connector engagement is more involved than ordinary accessory-wiring contact.

sections.title: Read the pair as a restraint circuit
sections.body: The positive and negative descriptions identify the two sides of the knee-airbag deployment circuit. They are not ordinary battery-supply and body-ground instructions. The face view and circuit identifiers support component identification; any handling or diagnosis belongs to the dedicated restraint-system procedure, which accounts for the RCM's stored backup energy.

topics.title: Luggage-lid release switch connection
topics.summary: The luggage-compartment lid release switch sends an electrical request to release the trunk latch. Connector C2610 also supports switch illumination, allowing the control to be visible separately from its release function.

sections.title: The switch starts a control request
sections.body: Pressing the switch changes an electrical input that the vehicle’s control system can interpret. The latch mechanism then performs the physical release when the relevant system conditions permit it. This distinction matters because the switch connection describes a request circuit, not the complete electrical path powering the latch actuator.

sections.title: Lighting and release have separate circuits
sections.body: The pinout identifies an instrument-panel structure ground, a switch-illumination circuit, and a decklid-release switch circuit. Illumination makes the control visible, while the release circuit communicates its use. A lit switch therefore does not establish that its request path or the downstream latch system is operating.

sections.title: Using the populated positions
sections.body: Several housing positions are unused, so the face view and function table should be read together. Circuit identifiers and wire colors distinguish the active paths. The connector reference helps locate the electrical interface, while the entry-system information explains how switch requests relate to the wider locking and release functions.

topics.title: Climate-control harness junction
topics.summary: The C263 inline connector joins harness 18B574 and harness 14401 for the cabin climate-control circuits shown. It carries electrical paths across the harness junction without acting as a control module itself.

sections.title: Airflow controls and sensors cross the junction
sections.body: The assignments include left and right temperature-door motors, recirculation and defrost-door circuits, and their position signals. These doors change air temperature blending or airflow direction. Evaporator and discharge-temperature sensing paths also appear, allowing the climate electronics to receive information about cooling and delivered air.

sections.title: Power paths differ from reference signals
sections.body: The junction includes the front-blower relay feed and an instrument-panel structure ground, alongside blower-control and voltage-reference circuits. The blower feed supplies operating energy, while control and sensor paths carry instructions or measurements. A voltage-reference return has a defined sensing role and should not be assumed interchangeable with the heavier body-ground circuit.

sections.title: Match circuits across both connector faces
sections.body: The male and female face views represent the two sides of the same junction. Some wire colors and sizes change between harnesses, so matching only by appearance can be misleading. Circuit identifiers and function descriptions establish continuity across the connector, while each face illustration provides the orientation needed to interpret its assignments.

topics.title: Harness Junction C264
topics.summary: C264 is an inline connector joining harness 14A005 with harness 14290. It carries multiple independent circuits across a separable junction so the two wiring assemblies can remain distinct parts of the vehicle harness.

sections.title: Each contact continues its own circuit
sections.body: Inside an inline connector, mating contacts continue individual conductors from one harness to the other. Sharing a housing does not connect those conductors together. A poor contact can interrupt one path while neighboring paths remain intact, which is why circuit identity matters more than the connector's overall appearance.

sections.title: The reference identifies both harness interfaces
sections.body: This page names the harness assemblies by their identifiers and provides a face view for each side. It does not supply descriptive circuit functions or named vehicle regions. Its useful role is therefore to establish the junction and contact correspondence without inventing a module, a mounting location or unsupported system assignments.

sections.title: Use circuit identifiers to follow the junction
sections.body: Compare the assigned circuit identifiers and wire descriptions across the two faces, keeping unassigned positions separate from populated ones. The connector-view orientation establishes how the faces correspond. A related system schematic is needed to determine which paths carry power, return, signals or communication and where they continue beyond these harnesses.

topics.title: The C265 harness junction
topics.summary: C265 joins harnesses 14A005 and 14290, carrying several independent circuits across one connection. Those circuits include protected power feeds, fuel-system controls and monitoring, and a vehicle communication pair.

sections.title: Several systems cross one junction
sections.body: The fuel-related paths include a fuel tank pressure reference and signal, canister vent control, and fuel pump command and monitor circuits. Each keeps its own electrical purpose as it crosses the connector. The junction simply continues these paths between harnesses; the connected controllers and components perform the actual sensing and control.

sections.title: Power and information share the housing
sections.body: The protected supply circuits deliver electrical energy, while command and sensor circuits carry operating information. The high-speed Controller Area Network (CAN) high and low wires form a communication pair. A connection problem can therefore affect different functions depending on which individual circuit loses its connection.

sections.title: Compare the mating harness faces
sections.body: The male and female views describe opposite sides of the same junction. Circuit identifiers and functions help match each path across it, even where listed wire sizes differ between harnesses. Connector-face orientation matters when interpreting the drawing, and the harness identifiers do not by themselves establish the connector's physical location.

topics.title: Right footwell ambient-light connection
topics.summary: The right-hand footwell lamp provides colored ambient illumination in the lower cabin. Connector C266 carries separate red, green and blue light-emitting diode (LED) channels and their shared negative connection.

sections.title: Color comes from combining light channels
sections.body: Red, green and blue LEDs can produce different perceived colors when their relative brightness changes. The connector gives each color its own positive circuit, allowing the ambient-lighting controller to influence the channels separately. The common negative connection completes their electrical paths within the arrangement shown by the lighting reference.

sections.title: Separate channels explain partial changes
sections.body: Because the colors have separate conductors, a circuit problem can change the color mixture rather than simply extinguish the whole lamp. That observation would still require diagnosis of the lamp, connection and control path. The shared negative connection matters to all the color channels, but it is labeled as a controller circuit.

sections.title: Distinguish light color from wire color
sections.body: Read the function column to identify which LED color a circuit serves; a wire's insulation color is a separate identification detail. The zone or non-zone wording belongs to the listed lighting assignments and does not establish every vehicle's equipment. The connector face supplies orientation, while the system diagram establishes the complete control arrangement.

topics.title: Brake pedal switch connector C278
topics.summary: C278 connects the brake pedal position (BPP) switch to the vehicle’s electrical circuits. The switch translates pedal movement into brake-applied and speed-control-deactivation information for systems that need to respond to braking.

sections.title: Pedal movement becomes an electrical state
sections.body: The switch changes electrical states as the brake pedal moves. This connector identifies a normally open brake on/off circuit and a separate speed-control-deactivation circuit. Those functions allow the car to recognize braking requests electrically, alongside the mechanical and hydraulic action that actually applies the wheel brakes.

sections.title: More than one brake-related signal
sections.body: The table includes a fused supply and a ground associated with the left front fender, as well as the switch-function circuits. Separating these paths matters because a supply or return interruption can affect what the receiving electronics see. A reported brake-input concern does not alone prove the pedal switch has failed.

sections.title: Interpret repeated assignments carefully
sections.body: Some assignments appear with alternative wire sizes, while the connector description and populated entries provide different kinds of information. The face view and applicable circuit drawing establish which arrangement belongs to the vehicle. “Normally open” describes a contact state, not an instruction to bridge the circuit or infer its complete switching sequence.

topics.title: Air inlet door actuator connections
topics.summary: The air inlet door actuator moves the climate system’s fresh-air and recirculation door. Connector C282 carries the motor-control and position-feedback circuits that let the controller move the door and monitor its position.

sections.title: The inlet door selects the air source
sections.body: Changing the inlet door position changes whether the blower draws outside air or recirculates cabin air. The actuator supplies the movement, while an internal position signal reports where the door has reached. Feedback lets the controller relate its movement command to the actual position instead of relying solely on elapsed motor operation.

sections.title: Why motor and feedback paths are separate
sections.body: The table identifies motor-control paths as well as a reference supply, reference return and recirculation-door position signal. The motor paths provide movement; the other circuits support position measurement. A connection problem can therefore affect either door motion or the controller’s knowledge of position, even though both functions share one actuator.

sections.title: Reading direction and reference labels
sections.body: The opening and closing descriptions are conditional on motor-circuit polarity as stated in the table. They should not be treated as ordinary fixed power and ground assignments. The unused connector position also matters when matching the face view. Both automatic and electronic manual climate overviews identify this actuator’s common inlet-door role.

topics.title: Sunload and ambient-light sensor connection
topics.summary: The sunload sensor assembly provides information about incoming sunlight, with separate left and right sunload signals in this connector reference. The same connection also includes ambient-light sensing paths used for automatic lighting.

sections.title: Sunshine adds heat without changing the set temperature
sections.body: Sunlight can warm an occupant and interior surfaces even when cabin air temperature changes little. Sunload information lets automatic climate control account for that added heat. The related dual automatic temperature control description includes this combined autolamp-sunload sensor; the connector alone does not make that climate-control equipment universal.

sections.title: One assembly supports different kinds of information
sections.body: The assignments distinguish right and left sunload signals from the ambient-light positive and negative paths. Ambient-light sensing concerns surrounding brightness for automatic lighting, while sunload information concerns the sunlight affecting cabin comfort. Separating these functions helps explain why a concern involving one function need not implicate every circuit in the connector.

sections.title: Read function labels before assigning power or ground
sections.body: Use the connector-face orientation and circuit descriptions to identify the relevant signal. A positive or negative sensor label does not, by itself, establish a battery feed or chassis ground. The associated system diagram supplies the wider electrical relationship; this page identifies how the named sensing paths pass through the connector.

topics.title: Autolamp sensor connector
topics.summary: An autolamp sensor detects ambient light so the lighting system can respond to changing brightness. This connector is titled autolamp and rain sensor, but its supplied assignments describe the day/night light-sensing circuit.

sections.title: Light level becomes an input
sections.body: An ambient-light sensor changes its electrical response as surrounding brightness changes. The lighting controller interprets that response when deciding whether exterior lighting is needed. This is a sensing function: the small sensor circuit provides information, while the lamp power circuits carry the current required to illuminate the lamps.

sections.title: The title has broader wording
sections.body: The assignment table names positive and negative ambient-light paths and marks other positions unused. It does not identify separate rain-sensing power or data circuits. Recognizing that limit prevents the combined connector title from being treated as evidence for a rain-sensor wiring arrangement that this page does not describe.

sections.title: Matching the ambient-light paths
sections.body: The connector face, wire colors and circuit identifiers link the named light-sensing functions to the physical connection. The positive and negative descriptions define the pair without establishing an independent battery feed. The related system schematic is needed to explain the controller interface and any additional functions of the installed assembly.

topics.title: The evaporator temperature-sensor connection
topics.summary: Connector C296 serves the air-conditioning (A/C) evaporator temperature sensor. The sensor reports the temperature of air leaving the evaporator so the control system can regulate cooling and prevent condensed moisture from freezing on the core.

sections.title: Cooling also removes moisture
sections.body: The evaporator absorbs heat from passing air, and moisture from that air condenses on its cold surfaces. If those surfaces become too cold, the moisture can freeze and obstruct airflow. Evaporator temperature information lets the powertrain control module (PCM) interrupt compressor operation when the discharge-air temperature indicates a freezing risk.

sections.title: Why the return circuit matters
sections.body: The connector table identifies an evaporator-temperature signal and a climate-control reference-return circuit. The return provides the electrical reference used to interpret the measurement; its label should not automatically be treated as an ordinary chassis-ground connection. An interrupted signal or return can make the temperature information unreliable without proving a refrigerant-system fault.

sections.title: Relating the connector to both climate systems
sections.body: Both manual and dual automatic temperature-control references describe evaporator-temperature information used for compressor control. Their message charts show the front controls interface module (FCIM) passing that information toward the PCM. The connector face identifies the local sensor interface, while the operating references explain how its measurement affects cooling.

topics.title: The blower motor's speed-control connection
topics.summary: Connector C297 serves the blower motor control module, which regulates the fan that moves air through the cabin climate unit. Its circuits separate the climate-control request from the electrical paths carrying and controlling blower-motor current.

sections.title: Airflow changes when motor speed changes
sections.body: The blower pushes air through the climate housing and into the cabin outlets. Changing its motor speed changes airflow, while heating and cooling depend on other components in the air path. The control module regulates motor current in response to a command, allowing requested airflow to differ from the electrical demand handled by the motor circuit.

sections.title: Why the command wire is distinct
sections.body: The table lists a climate blower-control signal, an instrument-panel ground, a front-blower relay circuit and a variable-speed blower-motor negative connection. The motor's return-side connection is part of current control. The command circuit conveys the requested operation, so it should not be interpreted as the conductor supplying the motor's working current.

sections.title: Recognizing active and unused cavities
sections.body: The housing includes cavities with no assigned circuit, alongside the active control and current-carrying connections. The face view establishes their orientation, and the wire-function table distinguishes their roles. This local connector reference explains the module interface; the wider climate schematic establishes the complete relay, motor and controller relationships.

topics.title: Upper left steering-wheel switch connections
topics.summary: The upper left steering-wheel switch assembly sends button requests while providing illumination for its controls. Connector C2998 separates the button-signal interface from the lighting feed and ground.

sections.title: Button information and lighting use different paths
sections.body: The analog-to-digital (A/D) channel label identifies an input through which control electronics can interpret a switch-related voltage. Its switch return completes that signal interface. Separate illumination feed and ground paths supply the button lighting, so illumination and button recognition are distinct electrical functions.

sections.title: Understand what an observation actually describes
sections.body: Illuminated buttons show that the lighting function is active, but they do not establish that a button request is reaching its receiving electronics. Likewise, a button can have a signal-path concern without identifying a lighting problem. The connector reference helps keep these observations tied to the appropriate circuit role.

sections.title: Use function labels where wire details are absent
sections.body: The supplied assignments use placeholders for circuit numbers and wire details, so the named functions and connector-face orientation carry the identification work. The page does not specify the individual button commands or their expected electrical values. Those details belong to the matching steering-wheel-control circuit and diagnostic reference.

topics.title: Upper right steering-wheel switch connection
topics.summary: Connector C2999 serves the upper switch assembly on the right side of the steering wheel. It carries the switch's control-signal path and separate illumination connections so the buttons can communicate inputs and remain visible.

sections.title: Button information travels as an electrical input
sections.body: The connector identifies an analog-to-digital (A/D) input channel and a right-side switch return. An analog input lets receiving electronics interpret an electrical level as control information. The page does not identify the individual button functions or the exact way each button changes that level.

sections.title: Lighting and switch operation use different paths
sections.body: An illumination feed and illumination ground serve the lighting within the switch assembly. Those paths are listed separately from the switch signal and return. This distinction matters because visible button lighting and successful command recognition depend on different electrical functions, even though they share a housing.

sections.title: Use the face view where wire details are absent
sections.body: The table leaves several wire-identification fields unspecified, making the connector-face orientation and function descriptions especially useful. The service-connector information identifies the matching connection hardware. Exact upstream routing and the receiving module belong in the associated circuit reference rather than being inferred from the switch's position on the wheel.

topics.title: Passenger belt pretensioner connection
topics.summary: A safety-belt pretensioner rapidly removes belt slack during a qualifying crash to help restrain the occupant sooner. Connector C303 carries the deployment circuit for the identified front-passenger outboard pretensioner.

sections.title: Rapid belt tightening supplements normal restraint
sections.body: The belt restrains the passenger through its webbing and attachment points, but slack delays how quickly it begins controlling body movement. A pyrotechnic pretensioner uses a rapid, one-time action to reduce that slack. It is a deployable safety device rather than an ordinary comfort adjustment motor.

sections.title: The paired wires serve one deployment circuit
sections.body: The table identifies positive and negative sides of the passenger pretensioner control circuit. These paths connect the device to its restraint-control electronics and must remain associated with the correct occupant position. Their labels describe a dedicated deployment interface, not a general-purpose power and ground connection.

sections.title: Identification does not authorize electrical testing
sections.body: The connector-face drawing, circuit names and harness information help distinguish this pretensioner from other belt-related components. They are reference information for the prescribed restraint-service process. Deployable-device connectors must not be probed or energized with test power, and a circuit concern should not be treated as proof that the pretensioner itself is defective.

topics.title: Passenger Occupant Classification Module Connection
topics.summary: The occupant classification system module (OCSM) evaluates passenger-seat information for the restraint system. Its connector carries operating power, a ground connection, communication circuits, and connections associated with passenger seat-belt tension.

sections.title: Turning seat information into restraint information
sections.body: Occupant classification gives the restraint system information about the passenger seat so restraint decisions can account for its occupant. Belt tension matters because a tightened belt can affect loading on the seat. The module interprets related inputs and shares information electronically with the vehicle.

sections.title: Separate paths serve separate jobs
sections.body: The connector identifies a supply available in RUN and START, a dedicated restraints ground, and a high-speed controller area network (CAN) pair. Supply and ground support module operation; the network carries messages. The seat-belt tension connections serve a sensing function, rather than supplying power to a seat motor.

sections.title: Reading the connector reference
sections.body: Use the connector-face illustration together with the function descriptions to distinguish power, communication, and sensor circuits. Wire colors help identify each listed circuit, but the illustrated orientation establishes its position. This reference identifies the module connection; it does not establish occupant-classification thresholds or provide a standalone restraint-system test.

topics.title: Parking brake switch connection
topics.summary: The parking brake switch reports the parking brake control's state electrically. Connector C306 carries its switch circuit and a ground path, allowing that state to be used by the vehicle's warning and control systems.

sections.title: Reporting movement rather than applying force
sections.body: Movement of the parking brake control changes the switch's electrical state. That gives the vehicle a way to recognize the control position, but the switch does not generate braking force. Its indication therefore describes a control state rather than directly measuring how firmly the parking brake holds the vehicle.

sections.title: Why the ground path matters
sections.body: The table identifies one switch-signal conductor and one ground conductor. Together they allow switch operation to change an electrical path that other circuitry can recognize. A break in the wiring or ground can affect the reported state without changing the mechanical position of the parking brake control.

sections.title: Understanding the location wording
sections.body: The ground description refers to the left cowl-side or A-pillar grounding area; it does not establish the switch's physical location. The connector face, circuit names, and wire colors identify this connection. The table supplies no complete operating truth table, so exact open-and-closed behavior belongs to the system reference.

topics.title: Left belt anchor pretensioner connection
topics.summary: The left front safety belt anchor pretensioner tightens the belt at its anchor when commanded during a qualifying crash. Connector C3065 carries the paired deployment-control circuits for this driver-side restraint component.

sections.title: Rapid tightening reduces belt slack
sections.body: A pretensioner uses a one-time pyrotechnic action to take up slack so the belt can restrain the occupant earlier. This entry identifies the anchor-mounted device, making the component name important when other pretensioners are also referenced in the manual. Its electrical connection supports activation rather than ordinary belt latching.

sections.title: Both conductors belong to the deployment loop
sections.body: The table identifies positive and negative control paths for the front driver-side pretensioner. Together they form the designated electrical loop to the deployable device. The negative label describes one side of that loop; it is not a general invitation to treat the conductor as a body-ground connection.

sections.title: Identification supports the prescribed restraint procedure
sections.body: The connector face, circuit identifiers and wire colors distinguish this connection from nearby restraint wiring. Service-connector entries describe available connection hardware, not permission to improvise a repair. Because the connected component is pyrotechnic, its inspection and handling must follow the specific supplemental restraint system instructions.

topics.title: Front passenger pretensioner connector
topics.summary: Connector C3066 serves the right-hand front safety-belt anchor and pretensioner assembly. The pretensioner rapidly takes up belt slack during a commanded restraint event, helping the belt engage the occupant earlier.

sections.title: A restraint actuator at the belt anchor
sections.body: The anchor provides a structural attachment for the belt, while the pretensioner adds an active tightening function. Its electrically initiated mechanism changes the belt’s effective slack during deployment. This function is separate from the retractor’s everyday task of storing webbing and allowing normal occupant movement.

sections.title: Why this is a dedicated circuit pair
sections.body: The connector table identifies positive and negative paths for the front passenger outboard pretensioner. These belong to its dedicated restraint circuit, rather than an ordinary accessory power-and-ground arrangement. Preserving circuit identity matters because the electrical connection is associated with a device intended to activate during a restraint event.

sections.title: Using the view for identification
sections.body: The connector face, harness designation, and wire descriptions identify the intended interface. They do not provide a complete restraint diagnostic or handling procedure, and the negative designation does not establish chassis ground. Any service interpretation belongs with the applicable restraint-system procedure rather than assumptions based on familiar-looking connector hardware.

topics.title: Passenger seat front tilt motor connection
topics.summary: The right-hand front tilt motor raises or lowers the front of the passenger seat cushion. Connector C3074 carries the electrical paths that let the seat adjustment switch command that movement.

sections.title: Changing the cushion angle
sections.body: The motor drives the seat’s front height adjustment mechanism. Moving the front upward or downward changes the cushion angle and the support beneath the occupant’s thighs. A reversible motor provides the two directions, with the electrical control changing how current passes through the motor.

sections.title: What the direction circuits do
sections.body: The populated circuit descriptions identify passenger front height down and front height up. These are the motor’s operating paths, so their roles relate to movement rather than digital communication. A poor connection can interrupt motor current even when the seat switch is being operated normally.

sections.title: Matching the connector to the motor
sections.body: Use the component heading, connector face and circuit descriptions together to identify this passenger seat connection. The table distinguishes used positions from unused ones; an empty position is not automatically a missing wire. Wire colors support identification, while the illustrated face establishes the orientation needed to interpret the assignments.

topics.title: Passenger Seat Height Motor Connection
topics.summary: Connector C3075 serves the right-hand front seat height-adjustment motor. Its listed circuits are associated with raising and lowering the rear of the passenger seat, changing the cushion’s position through the seat mechanism.

sections.title: Motor rotation becomes seat movement
sections.body: The electric motor turns a mechanical drive that moves the seat’s height mechanism. Reversing the electrical polarity across a typical reversible seat motor reverses its direction. This allows the same motor to produce upward or downward movement through the same gearing and linkage.

sections.title: Why neither direction label means permanent ground
sections.body: The table names passenger rear-height up and down circuits. Those names describe their roles in controlling movement, rather than establishing a fixed supply wire and a fixed ground wire. Their relationship across the motor determines direction, so each circuit must be understood as part of the paired motor connection.

sections.title: Distinguishing this motor from other seat adjustments
sections.body: The housing has unassigned positions alongside the working motor circuits. The rear-height wording is especially useful because a power seat can have separate mechanisms for other adjustments. The connector reference identifies this electrical connection; it does not establish that every seat movement concern originates in the motor rather than the switch, wiring or mechanism.

topics.title: Restraints controller connector
topics.summary: The restraints control module (RCM) evaluates crash-related inputs and commands appropriate restraint deployment. Connector C310A carries several of its sensor, power, indicator and deployment circuits, making correct circuit identification especially important.

sections.title: Inputs inform deployment decisions
sections.body: The RCM combines sensor information to decide whether particular restraints should deploy. This connector includes front impact sensor circuits and paired circuits for front and knee airbags, passenger airbag venting and the deployable steering column. These paths serve different purposes even though they share one connector housing.

sections.title: Power and deployment paths have different roles
sections.body: The fused supply supports module operation, while sensor circuits carry information and deployment circuits deliver controlled activation energy. Passenger airbag deactivation indicator entries also appear. A minus-marked deployment conductor is part of its designated pair; its label alone does not identify it as a general body ground.

sections.title: Read the connector face with its table
sections.body: The face drawing establishes cavity orientation, and the assignment table identifies each circuit by function, identifier and wire color. Used and unused entries help distinguish installed circuits from available housing positions. Because this connector serves deployable restraints, any diagnostic handling belongs within the specified restraint-system procedure.

topics.title: Restraints control module circuit connections
topics.summary: The restraints control module (RCM) monitors crash and occupant-related information and commands appropriate restraint deployment. Connector C310B groups several sensor, restraint-output, and communication circuits at that controller.

sections.title: Separating sensing from deployment
sections.body: The table includes side-impact sensors, seat-position sensors, and belt-buckle information alongside airbag and pretensioner outputs. Inputs describe conditions the module evaluates; outputs operate selected restraints when required. A connector containing both types needs careful identification because a sensor circuit and a deployment circuit have fundamentally different jobs.

sections.title: Understanding paired paths and messages
sections.body: Deployment feeds and returns form dedicated controlled circuits, so their negative labels should not be treated as ordinary body grounds. The high-speed Controller Area Network (CAN) pair provides a separate message path. Communication allows the module to exchange restraint information with other controllers rather than carrying deployment current.

sections.title: Reading the connector assignments
sections.body: Unused cavities and repeated alternative entries reflect the reference's circuit and terminal arrangements; they do not mean every variation appears together. Connector orientation and vehicle equipment determine the applicable assignment. This view supports identification, while restraint connection handling and circuit diagnosis remain governed by the dedicated supplemental restraint system procedures.

topics.title: Door-to-body harness junction C311
topics.summary: Inline connector C311 joins door-related harness 14631 with body harness 14A005. It carries circuits for locks, windows, mirrors, lighting, speakers, keyless-entry equipment and a side-impact sensor.

sections.title: Independent functions cross one junction
sections.body: A door contains both electrical loads and information sources. Window and mirror mechanisms need operating circuits, speakers receive audio, and latch or handle sensors report conditions. C311 brings these independent conductors through a detachable junction; the connector itself does not interpret a request or decide which device should operate.

sections.title: Shared packaging does not mean shared function
sections.body: Supply and ground circuits can support several door features, while individual signal paths serve specific devices. A connection concern can therefore affect one function or several, depending on the affected conductor. The listing also includes right-hand-drive alternatives, so driver and passenger descriptions must remain associated with their stated variant.

sections.title: Compare both faces by circuit identity
sections.body: The male and female tables identify opposite sides of the junction. Wire colors can change across it, making circuit identifiers and functions essential for matching conductors. Equipment-specific entries require the corresponding diagram. Side-impact sensor circuits belong to the restraint system, so their presence here is identification information rather than a general electrical-testing instruction.

topics.title: Left rear window motor connection
topics.summary: The left rear power-window motor converts electrical energy into movement of the window mechanism. Connector C3118 supplies the motor assembly and carries several opening, closing and coordinated-window control inputs.

sections.title: Motor rotation moves the glass
sections.body: A power-window motor drives the mechanism that raises or lowers the glass. The assembly needs enough electrical power to perform that mechanical work, plus a return path to complete the circuit. Control inputs tell it which movement is requested; those signals serve a different purpose from the main motor supply.

sections.title: Local and coordinated requests share the connection
sections.body: The table lists opening and closing switch circuits, a global-down control and a rear-left down command, alongside protected supplies and body ground. These names show that more than a simple pair of motor leads is involved. The connector reference does not define when each request takes priority or how internal control works.

sections.title: Identify each path by its function
sections.body: The face view belongs to harness 14A411, and the ground description names the left rear body area. Read the supply, return and command descriptions separately when interpreting the wiring. The page identifies an electrical interface; it does not establish a window initialization procedure or prove a motor fault from missing movement.

topics.title: The right rear window-motor connection
topics.summary: Connector C3119 carries electrical connections for the right rear power-window motor. The motor converts electrical energy into window movement, while the listed control circuits communicate requests such as opening, closing and coordinated lowering.

sections.title: Moving glass requires power and direction information
sections.body: The window motor drives the regulator mechanism that raises or lowers the glass. Operating power provides the energy for movement, while control inputs determine what movement is requested. The table lists fused feeds and a ground alongside command circuits, so these wires should not all be interpreted as interchangeable motor-power connections.

sections.title: Why several lowering commands are listed
sections.body: A window can respond to an individual control request or a coordinated vehicle request. The connector table distinguishes a global-down control circuit from a right-rear down circuit and also lists open and close switch circuits. These labels help separate the source of a movement request from the power needed to carry it out.

sections.title: Handling the left-labeled switch descriptions
sections.body: Although the component title identifies the right rear motor, two switch-circuit descriptions contain left open or close wording. Those labels should be retained as circuit identifiers and resolved through the illustrated wiring reference. They do not justify renaming the motor or assuming how the switch commands are distributed.

topics.title: Rear window harness junction C312
topics.summary: C312 joins harnesses 14A005 and 14A411 at an inline connection carrying rear-window-related circuits. Its assignments include protected supplies, window commands and a ground return associated with the left rear body area.

sections.title: Window commands cross the harness junction
sections.body: The table names left rear-window open and close functions, a rear-left window-motor down circuit and a global-down control circuit. These are distinct paths through the connector. Protected power supports the electrical equipment, while command circuits communicate requested action and the ground path provides an electrical return.

sections.title: A service junction between wiring sections
sections.body: An inline connector makes two harness sections separable without cutting their wires. Here, that separation brings several window-related paths into one housing. An interruption at the junction can prevent a command or supply from reaching its destination, which is why this reference matters alongside the window-system schematic.

sections.title: Do not assume both faces use identical labels
sections.body: Some circuit identifiers and colors differ between the male and female tables even where the function descriptions correspond. The face orientation and applicable wiring drawing are therefore essential to interpretation. The unused position is intentional in the listing, and the ground label does not establish the physical harness route.

topics.title: Door and mirror harness junction C313
topics.summary: C313 joins harnesses 14630 and 14A005, carrying a broad group of door, mirror, lighting and audio circuits. It provides a separable wiring junction for those functions rather than controlling them itself.

sections.title: Many independent circuits share the housing
sections.body: The assignments include window commands, door locks and latch status, mirror adjustment and folding, keyless-handle circuits, speaker pairs and lighting. Protected supplies and ground paths support the connected equipment. Separate terminals keep these functions electrically distinct even though their wires pass through the same inline connector.

sections.title: One junction spans several kinds of information
sections.body: A motor circuit carries operating current, a switch circuit communicates a request, and a speaker pair carries an audio signal. The page also includes side-impact sensor circuits. Recognizing these different roles prevents a door-related connector from being treated as a collection of interchangeable power wires.

sections.title: Variants and mating faces need careful matching
sections.body: The tables contain alternative assignments, wire colors and right-hand-drive (RHD) qualifiers on individual entries. Some descriptions differ between the mating faces. The relevant illustrated circuit and vehicle equipment determine the correct interpretation; neither a repeated cavity label nor adjacent text proves that all listed alternatives exist together.

topics.title: Window-Circuit Harness Junction: C314
topics.summary: C314 is an inline junction between harnesses 14A005 and 14A411 carrying window-related circuits. It passes supply, command and ground connections between harness sections without performing the window-control logic itself.

sections.title: Different window functions cross the junction
sections.body: The listed circuits include global window-down control, a rear-right window-down function and left open/close switch functions. These labels identify individual paths, not a complete description of the window mechanism. Their presence together does not establish that every vehicle uses every listed feature.

sections.title: Power and commands serve separate purposes
sections.body: Fused supply entries provide electrical energy, while command circuits communicate requested actions. The ground assignment references the right C-pillar or quarter-panel area. Keeping these functions distinct helps explain why a poor supply connection can affect operation differently from an interruption in a particular window command.

sections.title: Matching both halves of the connector
sections.body: The male and female face views describe the mating harness ends. Circuit identifiers allow corresponding paths to be followed across the junction, while unused positions remain separate from active wiring. The associated window schematic determines the exact operating relationships and equipment applicability beyond this connector’s assignments.

topics.title: Passenger Seatback Climate Harness Junction
topics.summary: C316 joins the passenger seatback climate-control harnesses. It carries the electrical paths for the blower, temperature sensing and the device that heats or cools the air delivered through the seatback.

sections.title: The seatback conditions air, then moves it
sections.body: The climate-controlled seat uses a blower assembly containing a fan and a Thermo-Electric Device (TED). The TED heats or cools incoming cabin air, and the blower sends that conditioned air through passages in the seat foam. The connector table calls the TED connections heater circuits, but this assembly supports both heating and cooling. Its separate blower-speed and temperature-sensor paths carry control and feedback information.

sections.title: Several circuit types cross one junction
sections.body: The connector brings these related functions together without acting as a control module itself. An interruption here can affect a power path, a control path or temperature feedback depending on the circuit involved. That is why identifying the actual circuit matters more than treating every connection as a heater feed.

sections.title: Compare the two harness faces
sections.body: The male and female tables show the mating sides of harnesses 14D233 and 14D230, with many housing positions unused. Circuit identifiers connect the climate-control device, blower and temperature-sensor paths across the junction. The two faces use different wire-detail entries in places, so keep each face associated with its listed harness. This connector reference does not establish its precise physical position within the seat.

topics.title: Auxiliary power-point connections
topics.summary: The auxiliary power point supplies vehicle electrical power to compatible accessories. Connector C319 provides its protected supply and instrument-panel ground return, with another connector position listed as unused.

sections.title: A supply and return complete the circuit
sections.body: An accessory draws current from the power point’s supply and returns it through the ground path. Both connections are needed for operation. Resistance at either connection can reduce the voltage available to the accessory under load, even though the power point appears mechanically intact from inside the cabin.

sections.title: Why circuit protection appears in the table
sections.body: The supply entry identifies a fuse-or-circuit-breaker source, while the return entry identifies an instrument-panel structure ground. Protection limits the consequences of excessive current in the circuit. The connector reference therefore helps separate the outlet itself from its supply, protection and return path when interpreting the wider wiring information.

sections.title: Understanding the unused position
sections.body: The shell includes an unused position, so the housing’s size does not imply that every position carries a circuit. Match the illustrated face to the function and wire-color descriptions. This page does not establish when the outlet is powered or its permitted accessory load; those details belong to the applicable system reference.

topics.title: Right front seat control switch
topics.summary: The right front seat control switch provides electrical control of the passenger-seat adjustments listed in this reference. Its connector carries a power feed, ground and separate circuits for track movement and cushion-height changes.

sections.title: How the controls change seating position
sections.body: Forward and rearward circuits concern movement along the seat track. Front-height and rear-height circuits change the support position at different parts of the cushion, altering height or tilt. The switch directs the requested adjustment through the corresponding electrical path rather than treating every seat movement as one function.

sections.title: Why common and individual paths matter
sections.body: Power and ground support the switch’s operation, while the movement circuits distinguish its outputs. A common connection concern can affect several adjustments, whereas one movement circuit has a more specific role. This relationship helps organize an electrical investigation without assuming that a seat-motion concern proves the switch is defective.

sections.title: Matching the passenger-seat reference
sections.body: Use the connector-face illustration with the passenger-seat function descriptions, including the positions marked unused. Similar switch housings can have different circuit assignments, so appearance alone is insufficient. This entry identifies the listed right-seat adjustments; it does not establish additional functions simply because another seat-switch reference includes them.

topics.title: Driver buckle switch connection
topics.summary: The driver safety belt buckle holds the belt tongue and includes an electrical indication of buckle status. Connector C3201 carries the buckle-sensor circuit and its ground return so the vehicle can use that status for the seat belt reminder.

sections.title: A mechanical latch also supplies information
sections.body: The buckle's latch secures the belt mechanically, while its electrical switch reports the buckle condition. These are related but separate functions. A connection problem can prevent reliable status information even when the tongue physically latches, so electrical diagnosis needs to distinguish the signal path from the buckle's mechanical action.

sections.title: The signal depends on a return path
sections.body: The assignment table names a driver-side seat belt reminder sensor circuit and a driver-seat restraints ground. Together they provide the electrical interface for buckle status. An interruption in either path can affect the information seen by the receiving electronics; the connector page alone does not establish the cause.

sections.title: Housing positions and installed circuits differ
sections.body: The connector housing contains positions that are listed as unused as well as the active circuits. The face view establishes orientation, while the table identifies function and wire color. Service-lead details identify connector repair hardware; they do not replace the restraint-system diagnostic instructions governing any work on this connection.

topics.title: Driver-seat restraint harness junction
topics.summary: C3206 is an inline junction between harness sections carrying driver-seat restraint circuits. It provides a separable connection for the listed seat-mounted side-airbag wiring and associated entries in the harness reference.

sections.title: A junction within restraint wiring
sections.body: The page identifies harnesses 14C687/14D232 on one face and 14D231 on the other. Their listed circuits serve driver-seat side-airbag functions, with a belt-tension sensor entry also appearing in the male-face data. The junction carries these circuits between harness sections; it does not interpret sensor information or decide deployment.

sections.title: Why circuit identity matters here
sections.body: The airbag entries include paired positive and negative circuit designations. These belong to controlled restraint circuits and must not be interpreted as ordinary accessory power and body ground. A connection problem can alter the circuit condition seen by restraint electronics, making accurate identification essential before following the appropriate service information.

sections.title: Reading both connector faces
sections.body: The extracted male-face table repeats positions and includes alternative circuit descriptions, while the female-face table presents a different set of entries. Those rows cannot safely be flattened into one universal assignment. Use the illustrated face, harness identification, and applicable restraint reference together; this connector page is an identification aid.

topics.title: Coupe left B-pillar side-impact sensor
topics.summary: The left B-pillar side-impact sensor supplies crash information to the restraints control module (RCM). The wiring diagram places this sensor in the coupe-only branch. It is an electronic sensing device, separate from the airbags that the controller may deploy.

sections.title: A sensor helps the controller understand the impact
sections.body: The pillar-mounted side-impact sensors measure vehicle acceleration, meaning how quickly its motion changes. The door-mounted side-impact sensors use a different input: pressure changes inside the door. The RCM evaluates crash inputs to decide which restraints to activate; a sensor is not a mechanical trigger for one nearby airbag.

sections.title: Keep the coupe and door-sensor branches separate
sections.body: The connector title identifies the left-hand B-pillar sensor, while its circuit descriptions use driver-side row-two wording. The matching wiring diagram shows both B-pillar sensors inside a coupe-only boundary. The door sensors sit outside that boundary, so the coupe label should not be extended to every sensor on the sheet. These names identify the component and circuit; they do not establish a rear-seat airbag.

sections.title: What the two wires do
sections.body: Cavity 1 carries circuit VR219, the sensor feed shown in the wiring diagram. Cavity 2 carries RR133, its dedicated sensor return. Both are listed in harness 14A005. This is a monitored sensing connection, not an airbag deployment loop or a general accessory power connection. Use the face view to identify it, and follow the SRS diagnostic sequence for testing; the manual explicitly says not to probe impact sensors with a multimeter.

topics.title: Coupe right B-pillar side-impact sensor
topics.summary: The right B-pillar side-impact sensor supplies crash information to the restraints control module (RCM). The wiring diagram places this sensor in the coupe-only branch. It is an electronic sensing device, separate from the airbags that the controller may deploy.

sections.title: A sensor helps the controller understand the impact
sections.body: The pillar-mounted side-impact sensors measure vehicle acceleration, meaning how quickly its motion changes. The door-mounted side-impact sensors use a different input: pressure changes inside the door. The RCM evaluates crash inputs to decide which restraints to activate; a sensor is not a mechanical trigger for one nearby airbag.

sections.title: Keep the coupe and door-sensor branches separate
sections.body: The connector title identifies the right-hand B-pillar sensor, while its circuit descriptions use passenger-side row-two wording. The matching wiring diagram shows both B-pillar sensors inside a coupe-only boundary. The door sensors sit outside that boundary, so the coupe label should not be extended to every sensor on the sheet. These names identify the component and circuit; they do not establish a rear-seat airbag.

sections.title: What the two wires do
sections.body: Cavity 1 carries circuit VR220, the sensor feed shown in the wiring diagram. Cavity 2 carries RR134, its dedicated sensor return. Both are listed in harness 14A005. This is a monitored sensing connection, not an airbag deployment loop or a general accessory power connection. Use the face view to identify it, and follow the SRS diagnostic sequence for testing; the manual explicitly says not to probe impact sensors with a multimeter.

topics.title: Left power lumbar motor connection
topics.summary: The power lumbar assembly adjusts the support behind the occupant’s lower back. Connector C3215 joins its motor to the left-seat wiring. The Mustang’s diagnostic procedure identifies this as a motor connection whose polarity changes with the requested direction of adjustment.

sections.title: Electrical direction changes the support adjustment
sections.body: The motor operates the support mechanism within the backrest, rather than moving the entire seat along its floor track. The manual lists the lumbar motor as part of the power lumbar assembly, which is serviced as a unit. Reversing the electrical polarity lets the motor operate in the opposite direction when the seat control switch requests the opposite adjustment.

sections.title: Keep the circuit labels separate from the actual hardware
sections.body: Terminal A carries CPS19 and terminal B carries CPS18. The connector table calls these a deflate-solenoid circuit and a lumbar-pump circuit, but the Mustang pinpoint test explicitly names C3215 as the driver seat lumbar motor. It traces terminal A to C352 cavity 3 and terminal B to C352 cavity 4. Those source labels should not be used to invent a separate pneumatic pump or air-cell valve.

sections.title: What this reference helps identify
sections.body: The connector face and wire descriptions distinguish the two motor paths in harness 14D232. Because their polarity changes with direction, neither should be treated as a permanently fixed body-ground lead. The seat also contains side-airbag wiring, so the dedicated seat diagnostic procedure’s SRS handling sequence remains important when working in this area. The connection table identifies the interface; it does not establish that a nonmoving lumbar support needs a new motor.

topics.title: Driver belt pretensioner connection
topics.summary: The driver safety belt pretensioner rapidly takes up belt slack during a qualifying crash. Connector C323 identifies the dedicated electrical pair used to activate the named driver-side restraint device.

sections.title: Tightening begins early in the crash
sections.body: A pretensioner uses a pyrotechnic mechanism to shorten part of the belt system quickly. Taking up slack brings the belt into effective contact with the occupant sooner, helping the belt manage forward movement. It works with the belt’s restraint function and is different from the everyday buckle switch.

sections.title: A dedicated pair serves deployment
sections.body: The table labels positive and negative driver-pretensioner control paths. These belong to a deployment circuit, rather than an ordinary accessory supply and body ground. Correct component and circuit identification matters because the restraint controller must monitor and command the intended device, even when nearby restraint connectors look similar.

sections.title: Use the face view for identification
sections.body: The reference identifies this connection in harness 14A005 and includes restraint-specific service-lead information. It does not describe a deployment test or establish a safe handling sequence. Restraint service procedures govern that work; the connector view is not a basis for applying power or performing ordinary electrical probing.

topics.title: Passenger belt buckle connector C3238
topics.summary: C3238 connects electrical circuits associated with the passenger safety belt buckle and belt-tension sensing. These circuits report belt-related information while the buckle’s mechanical latch physically retains the belt tongue.

sections.title: Buckle status and belt tension differ
sections.body: A buckle-status signal indicates whether the belt is latched, while a tension sensor responds to force in the belt. These are different observations about the same restraint system. The connector table includes both functions, so the connector’s buckle title should not be read as describing only a simple buckle switch.

sections.title: Separate signals need reliable returns
sections.body: The assignments identify a buckle reminder signal, belt-tension sensor circuits and passenger-seat restraints clean grounds. The tension-sensor entries distinguish a sensor signal from a positive control-module connection. The ground paths provide electrical references and returns; a disrupted reference can affect the information received even when the buckle still latches mechanically.

sections.title: Match the function to the connector face
sections.body: The face view establishes cavity orientation, while the table names the circuit carried at each populated position. An unused entry is not automatically a missing wire. This reference identifies the harness interface; the applicable restraint diagnostic procedure determines how its circuits are evaluated without treating a signal concern as proof of buckle failure.

topics.title: Passenger seat position sensor connection
topics.summary: The right-hand seat position sensor reports information about the passenger seat’s position on its track. Connector C3240 carries the position-sensing circuit and its designated restraint-system ground return.

sections.title: Seat position becomes restraint information
sections.body: Moving a seat changes the occupant’s position relative to the surrounding restraint equipment. A seat-track position sensor converts a mechanical position condition into an electrical indication for the restraint system. It senses position; it does not provide the motor power that moves the seat.

sections.title: Keep position feedback distinct from seat adjustment
sections.body: The circuit table specifically names passenger seat-track position and a passenger-seat restraints clean ground. Those labels distinguish this connection from seat motor or comfort-feature wiring. A designated sensing return provides the electrical reference for the measurement, so return-path condition matters alongside the position-signal path.

sections.title: Read this as identification, not a test plan
sections.body: Use the connector face and function table to understand which circuit is the sensing path and which is its return. The page does not define the sensor’s switching threshold or restraint strategy. Those details belong to the dedicated system reference, whose handling instructions govern work around restraint-related connections.

topics.title: Selector lever electrical connections
topics.summary: The automatic-transmission selector lever combines mechanical range selection with electrical functions such as Park detection and the brake shift interlock. Connector C3245 carries the circuits that support those functions and illuminate the selector controls.

sections.title: Mechanical selection with electrical supervision
sections.body: A cable links the selector lever to the transmission’s manual control lever. Within the selector assembly, the brake shift interlock mechanically blocks movement out of Park until the required release conditions are met. Park detection supplies position information, while the illumination circuit makes the controls visible in low light.

sections.title: Why these circuits share a connector
sections.body: The connector table identifies Park-detect, interlock-control, illumination and instrument-panel ground circuits at one assembly. These paths perform different jobs: a position circuit communicates a state, an actuator circuit controls movement, and ground provides an electrical return. A concern involving the lever therefore needs the matching circuit information.

sections.title: Matching the function to the connector face
sections.body: Use the illustrated face orientation with the function and wire-color columns to identify the relevant path. The listed ground entries and unused position are part of that identification. The connector view maps the assembly’s interface; the external-controls description explains when the interlock should release and how the selector linkage works.

topics.title: Power-folding mirror relay connection
topics.summary: The power-folding mirror relay participates in switching the mirrors between folded and driving positions. Connector C3276 identifies its supply, ground, toggle-switch input, and fold-related control circuits.

sections.title: Translating a request into switching
sections.body: Power-folding mirrors use electrical actuation to move the mirror housings. A relay provides controlled switching within that system, allowing a request circuit to influence an operating circuit. The connector names fold-position and drive-position functions, showing that the reference concerns housing movement rather than adjustment of the mirror glass.

sections.title: Why each connection has a distinct role
sections.body: The table identifies a protected power supply, a right cowl or pillar ground, and a fold/drive toggle-switch circuit. Those support operation and the driver’s request, while the remaining circuits are labeled for the two mirror positions. An interruption at the connection can prevent the intended switching relationship.

sections.title: Leaving internal operation to the schematic
sections.body: The face view and circuit identifiers establish which harness wires belong at this relay connection. They do not show its internal switching arrangement or the complete mirror-motor circuit. The illustrated wiring reference is needed to interpret those paths, rather than assuming a familiar relay layout from the housing alone.

topics.title: Auxiliary audio input connection
topics.summary: The audio input socket accepts an external player’s analog sound signal for the vehicle’s audio system. C3312 connects that socket to the harness through separate stereo signal paths and an associated return connection.

sections.title: How sound travels through the socket
sections.body: An analog audio signal is a small changing voltage that represents sound. Separate left and right channels preserve stereo information, allowing sounds to differ between the speakers. The return connection provides the electrical reference needed to interpret those changing voltages at the receiving audio equipment.

sections.title: Why channel identity matters
sections.body: This reference distinguishes the right positive signal, left positive signal and the connection labeled left or common negative. An interrupted signal path can affect audio without interrupting power to the radio. The connector assignments therefore help separate an input-signal concern from the audio system’s main power supply.

sections.title: Matching the socket to its wiring
sections.body: The connector face and wire-color entries identify the assigned contacts, while an unassigned cavity is shown separately. The service-pigtail information describes replacement wiring hardware. None of the listed assignments identifies a charging supply or digital data connection; this page concerns the socket’s analog audio interface.

topics.title: Right front seat-track motor connection
topics.summary: The right-hand front seat-track motor moves the seat forward and rearward along its tracks. Connector C332 provides the motor’s directional operating circuits from the passenger-seat adjustment controls.

sections.title: Turning motor rotation into seat travel
sections.body: The track mechanism converts electric-motor rotation into movement along the seat rails. Reversing the motor’s direction reverses seat travel. For a reversible motor circuit, the switching arrangement changes electrical polarity across the motor connections, so the two directional wires should not be assumed to be permanent power and permanent ground.

sections.title: Why this connection carries operating current
sections.body: The table identifies passenger forward and rearward adjustment functions. These circuits serve the motor’s movement rather than describing a position-data network. Resistance at a motor connection can reduce the voltage available under load, while an interruption can prevent current from completing its path through the motor.

sections.title: Distinguishing housing size from active wiring
sections.body: The connector housing includes unused positions alongside the two listed motor circuits. The face view and wire identifiers establish which connections are active. This page identifies the motor interface; a seat that will not move still needs the relevant diagnosis to distinguish an electrical concern from a mechanical track problem.

topics.title: Cup-holder ambient-light connection
topics.summary: The floor-console cup-holder ambient lamp provides colored accent lighting around the cup holders. Connector C3349 carries separate red, green, and blue lighting circuits plus their shared negative connection.

sections.title: How one lamp produces several colors
sections.body: The lamp uses light-emitting diode (LED) channels for red, green, and blue. Changing their relative output creates different perceived colors. Because each color has its own circuit, losing one channel can alter the available color combinations even when the lamp still produces visible light.

sections.title: Color circuits and the shared return
sections.body: The table identifies three module-controlled positive channels and one common negative channel. A problem on an individual color path can affect that color, while a problem on the shared path can affect the whole lamp. The negative designation describes the lighting circuit and does not independently establish a chassis-ground connection.

sections.title: Reading the connector by function
sections.body: The face view matches each wire to its color-channel function, circuit identifier, and terminal information. Its zone-or-non-zone wording describes the listed circuit application without establishing the entire lighting configuration. This reference helps identify the connection; a color complaint still needs diagnosis of the lamp, wiring, and controlling electronics.

topics.title: Driver-side scuff plate lighting
topics.summary: The illuminated driver-side scuff plate adds colored light at the door opening. Its connector carries separate color channels and a shared return path for the lamp's light-emitting diodes (LEDs).

sections.title: Combining the color channels
sections.body: Red, green, and blue light can be combined in different proportions to produce different visible colors. The connector assigns a separate positive circuit to each color channel. Changing their relative output changes the lamp's appearance, while the listed negative path completes the electrical circuit for the lighting.

sections.title: Recognizing the ambient-light connection
sections.body: The positive circuits are identified with ambient lighting zone 3, and the return carries a broader zone or non-zone description. This reference therefore identifies a controlled lighting interface. Its negative label should be interpreted through the lighting circuitry rather than assumed to mean an independent local body ground.

sections.title: Reading functions before colors
sections.body: The table distinguishes wire color from the color of light being controlled. Those descriptions answer different questions: one identifies a conductor, and the other identifies its lighting function. Match the connector face with the circuit descriptions to keep the color channels and their shared return correctly associated.

topics.title: Passenger scuff-plate ambient lighting
topics.summary: The passenger scuff-plate lamp illuminates the trim at the door opening as part of the ambient-lighting system. Connector C3370 carries the separate color-channel feeds and the lamp's electrical return.

sections.title: How separate colors create the light
sections.body: The assignments identify red, green and blue light-emitting diode channels. Changing the contribution of those colors changes the combined light seen at the scuff plate. Each channel needs a complete current path, so a problem affecting one channel can change the resulting color without extinguishing every part of the lamp.

sections.title: What the connector brings together
sections.body: The positive color feeds are identified separately from the common negative lighting connection. These are lamp-control paths, rather than a listed digital communication pair. The negative connection is described through the lighting control system, so the table should not be simplified into an assumed direct connection to nearby body metal.

sections.title: Reading channel and zone descriptions
sections.body: The color feeds and return carry different zone wording in the assignment table. Those labels need to remain attached to their individual circuits rather than being rewritten as one universal zone description. The face view and circuit colors identify the connection; the related wiring establishes the controlling paths.

topics.title: The passenger-seat harness junction
