sections.title: Illumination and lock indication serve different purposes
sections.body: The handle ambient lamp makes the interior handle easier to see, while the door-lock indicator communicates lock status. Although both appear within the same door-related assembly, their circuit functions should remain distinct. A lighting concern therefore needs to be related to the correct function rather than assumed to involve the door latch.

sections.title: Control and return paths cross the door connections
sections.body: The drawing includes the body control module (BCM), Body Control Module B, a return connection, and a delayed-accessory output marked as a field-effect transistor (FET). Harness junctions carry these circuits toward both front doors. A return path completes the relevant circuit, while a controlled output determines when electrical energy is available.

sections.title: Following the without-memory version
sections.body: The equipment note limits this sheet to vehicles without memory. Left-hand and right-hand lamp labels identify the two door branches, and continuation references connect them to other remote keyless entry and alarm sheets. Repeated wire colors alone are insufficient for tracing; the circuit identifiers distinguish their electrical roles.

topics.title: Driver-door lock and memory commands
topics.summary: This remote-entry and alarm sheet shows driver-door controls and their relationship to the driver door module (DDM) in the memory-equipped arrangement. It includes lock, unlock, memory-setting, illumination, power, ground, and communication circuits.

sections.title: Switches request actions
sections.body: A door switch provides an electrical input indicating the occupant’s chosen action. The DDM interprets the relevant inputs as part of coordinating door functions. The labeled memory-setting inputs are requests associated with stored settings; their presence does not mean the switch itself drives a seat or mirror motor.

sections.title: Why the module has several circuit types
sections.body: The battery junction box (BJB) supplies a protected feed, while the ground supports the return path. Medium-speed controller area network (MS-CAN) connections allow message exchange with other electronics. Illumination and switch-return labels describe additional circuit roles that should be distinguished from motor power or network data.

sections.title: Keeping equipment branches in context
sections.body: MEMORY is the heading for this sheet. The small dashed coupe outline marks the C535 connection on the return path to the master window control switch; it does not restrict the entire sheet to coupes. The illustrated lines and continuation markers connect the door controls to their supporting diagrams. Keep this connector qualification separate from the overall memory-equipment configuration.

topics.title: Memory-equipped passenger-door lock controls
topics.summary: This sheet shows passenger-door controls for the memory-equipped arrangement in the remote-entry and alarm wiring reference. It brings together the passenger door module, lock switch, window-control references and their supporting electrical paths.

sections.title: The door module’s role
sections.body: The passenger door module (PDM) provides local electronics for door functions. Lock and unlock switch inputs communicate the occupant’s request, while illumination makes the controls visible. Power and ground allow the module to operate; network connections let door electronics exchange information with the rest of the vehicle.

sections.title: Why window wiring appears here
sections.body: The passenger window control and door-lock controls occupy the same door and appear together with their return circuits. This sheet helps distinguish a switch request from the supply that supports the electronics. It also identifies the body control module (BCM) and a protected supply labeled hot at all times.

sections.title: Read the page scope and local branches
sections.body: The MEMORY heading specifies the arrangement for this whole sheet. The medium-speed Controller Area Network pair carries messages rather than directly powering a lock motor. Follow the drawn wires and continuation references to distinguish lock and unlock inputs, illumination, switch returns and the module ground. Window references connect these shared door interfaces to their companion circuits.

topics.title: Memory-equipped driver-door latch wiring
topics.summary: The remote-entry and alarm system needs both lock actuation and information about whether doors are closed. This memory-equipped sheet shows left-front latch circuits alongside body-control, door-control and center-console-lock references.

sections.title: Lock commands and door status serve different jobs
sections.body: The latch motor performs electrical locking work, while the door-ajar switch reports latch-related door status. The body control module (BCM) includes labeled driver-unlock and auxiliary-lock relay functions. The page explicitly states that its door-ajar switches are electrically closed when the corresponding door is closed.

sections.title: Related door functions meet on this sheet
sections.body: The MEMORY heading applies to the whole sheet. Within that configuration, a separate dashed locking-bin box identifies the center-console lock assembly and its connections. The driver door module and window-regulator motor also appear through related door circuits. These references help follow signals between functions; the local locking-bin box does not establish that every memory-equipped car has that optional assembly.

sections.title: Read relay and switch labels literally
sections.body: The relays labeled non-serviceable are identified as part of the module arrangement shown. Door-ajar switch state must be interpreted using the page's explicit closed-door note, not an assumption based on the word “ajar.” Continuation letters, connector identifiers and ground references carry the circuits onward without describing their physical wiring route.

topics.title: Memory-equipped passenger-door latch wiring
topics.summary: This memory-equipped entry-system sheet covers electrical functions associated with the right front door latch and passenger-door equipment. It distinguishes lock actuation, door-ajar information, power supply and related module connections.

sections.title: Moving the latch and reporting door state
sections.body: The latch motor performs an electrical actuation function, while the door-ajar switch reports whether the door is closed. Those are separate jobs even when associated with the same latch assembly. The sheet explicitly states that the door-ajar switches are electrically closed when the doors are physically closed.

sections.title: Why modules and the window motor appear
sections.body: The body control module (BCM) contains the labeled central lock and unlock relays, and the passenger door module (PDM) and window-regulator motor also appear on the sheet. Their presence provides context for door-related circuits. The relays are marked non-serviceable, which describes their service status within the module.

sections.title: Read the page scope and local branches
sections.body: The MEMORY heading applies to the complete sheet. Continuations, connector names and ground references establish where each circuit proceeds within this arrangement. The continuously powered labels describe supply availability; they do not mean a motor runs continuously. Use the actual drawn connections and splice dots to follow the latch, passenger door module and window-related paths.

topics.title: Door Lock Indicator and Handle Lighting
topics.summary: This remote-entry sheet shows electrical connections for door-lock indicators and interior door-handle ambient lamps. The diagram is marked for the memory-equipped arrangement and includes both door modules and body control module B.

sections.title: Light reports status rather than moving the lock
sections.body: A door-lock indicator provides visible information about locking status, while ambient handle lighting makes the handle area visible. These lighting functions differ from the actuator that physically moves a lock. The sheet's status and return labels help separate indication circuits from the mechanical locking function.

sections.title: Both doors share part of the circuit structure
sections.body: The driver door module (DDM) and passenger door module (PDM) each have a status-labeled connection. Body control module B provides the named return relationship, with a splice connecting branches. Showing both doors together makes the shared path visible while preserving the separate status connection for each side.

sections.title: Follow status, return and continuation labels
sections.body: Left-hand and right-hand lamp connectors are identified separately, and continuation marks link this page with the rest of the entry-and-alarm circuitry. Follow those labels rather than interpreting every brown wire as the same function. The memory qualification limits applicability and does not establish the layout of vehicles without that equipment.

topics.title: Hood and Trunk Ajar Signals
topics.summary: The hood switch and luggage compartment latch provide electrical information about whether those openings are secured. This alarm-system sheet shows the status circuits associated with the body control module (BCM).

sections.title: Movement becomes an electrical status
sections.body: Opening or closing the hood changes the hood switch's electrical state. The luggage compartment latch likewise provides trunk-ajar information. These inputs let the BCM distinguish an opening that is secured from one reported open, which matters when the vehicle monitors its perimeter.

sections.title: Separate the opening from its reported state
sections.body: The mechanical latch holds an opening shut, while the electrical circuit reports its condition. A disagreement between those two things can involve the switch, latch sensing arrangement, wiring or connections. This sheet exists to identify that reporting path rather than establish which component has failed.

sections.title: Follow the illustrated branches
sections.body: The reference identifies hood-ajar and trunk-ajar inputs, connectors, grounds and a splice. Follow the drawn lines to establish their relationships; nearby text alone does not show a connection. The note excluding the 5.0L automatic-transmission combination belongs to its illustrated branch, so its exact scope matters.

topics.title: Keyless Entry Radio Module Circuits
topics.summary: This sheet shows the Radio Transceiver Module (RTM) within the remote keyless-entry and alarm system. It connects the radio interface to operating power, ground and communication paths used by the vehicle’s electronic controls.

sections.title: Radio communication meets vehicle wiring
sections.body: A transceiver handles radio communication, allowing information from a remote device to enter the vehicle’s electronic system without a physical wire to the key. The RTM’s wired connections then link that radio function with the rest of the car. Its presence does not mean it directly powers every lock or alarm device.

sections.title: Power and two communication paths
sections.body: The sheet identifies a fused battery supply, ground and Medium-Speed Controller Area Network (MS-CAN) pair. It also shows a separate K-line connection to the Body Control Module (BCM). These paths have different purposes: power operates the module, while the communication connections carry information between electronic components.

sections.title: Understanding supply availability and continuations
sections.body: Hot at all times describes the availability of the battery supply, which supports functions needed while the vehicle is parked. It does not mean every associated output is continuously active. Network continuation references lead to the wider communication diagrams, while connector and ground identifiers tie this sheet to the corresponding physical reference views.

topics.title: Passive-key antenna wiring
topics.summary: Passive-key antennas create localized electromagnetic fields used during communication with a compatible vehicle key. This sheet identifies a front passive anti-theft system (PATS) antenna, a rear keyless-entry antenna and their body control module (BCM) connections.

sections.title: An antenna supports key communication
sections.body: An antenna converts changing electrical current into an electromagnetic field that a nearby compatible key can respond to. That supports the vehicle's key-recognition process. The front anti-theft and rear keyless-entry names identify different antenna roles, but the sheet does not describe the entire authorization sequence or every communication device involved.

sections.title: Paired drive circuits create the field
sections.body: The antenna connections are labeled positive and negative, with corresponding high and low half-bridge output descriptions at the BCM. A half-bridge is an electronic switching arrangement used to control a circuit's electrical drive. These paired outputs should be understood as antenna-drive connections, rather than assumed to be constant power and body ground.

sections.title: Match each antenna to its illustrated pair
sections.body: Use the component names, circuit identifiers and drawn lines to establish which BCM output pair serves each antenna. Connector and location references support that identification. A key-recognition concern can involve the communication path or other system conditions, so this wiring sheet alone does not establish that an antenna is defective.

topics.title: Exterior handle keyless-entry circuits
topics.summary: This sheet covers electrical connections associated with the left and right exterior front-door handles. It shows handle power and ground labels alongside antenna circuits used by the keyless-entry system to communicate near the doors.

sections.title: The handle has an electrical role
sections.body: The exterior handle is part of the physical door-opening mechanism, but its listed electrical connections also support keyless access. An antenna creates a local communication field used in recognizing a nearby key. Handle power and ground support electrical operation, while the antenna pair serves a different purpose from an ordinary lamp or motor feed.

sections.title: Why the body controller appears here
sections.body: The body control module (BCM) is shown with separate exterior-antenna output labels and half-bridge designations. A half-bridge is an electronic switching arrangement used to drive an electrical load. Here those labels concern antenna drive, so the positive and negative antenna connections should be understood as a controlled pair.

sections.title: Distinguishing the two door branches
sections.body: The left and right handle names identify separate branches that may look similar at first glance. Connector references and wire identifiers distinguish them and show how to continue tracing the illustrated circuits. The drawing establishes connections; the order of the extracted labels does not establish which controller output reaches a particular handle.

topics.title: Alarm Intrusion Sensing and Security Horn Wiring
topics.summary: This sheet connects overhead-console intrusion sensing with the body control module and the security horn relay. It shows the electrical support and communication paths used by these alarm components.

sections.title: Detection and warning have separate roles
sections.body: Intrusion sensing provides information about activity inside the vehicle, while the security horn provides an audible alarm output. The body control module (BCM) is part of the control relationship shown here. A detection concern and a horn concern can therefore involve different branches of the same alarm system.

sections.title: Recognizing supply, ground, and communication
sections.body: Battery voltage, marked VBATT, supplies electrical energy; ground, marked GND, completes the supply circuit. The Local Interconnect Network (LIN) connection carries communication rather than horn operating current. The always-live supply labels explain how alarm-related circuits can remain powered with the ignition off, without implying that every component is continuously active.

sections.title: Using the sheet as an electrical map
sections.body: Connector identifiers, wire colors, circuit labels, and the shared ground reference let you follow connections into other sheets. The security horn relay is identified as non-serviceable. Unused connections should remain distinct from active circuits, and the schematic’s arrangement describes electrical relationships rather than the physical route of the harness.

topics.title: The tire pressure system's wired connections
topics.summary: Tire pressure monitoring uses pressure information from the wheels to support warnings about inflation. This diagram concentrates on the radio transceiver module and its wired supply, ground, and communication connections within that system.

sections.title: Wireless information still needs wired support
sections.body: Wheel pressure information reaches the vehicle by radio, but the receiving electronics depend on ordinary vehicle wiring. The radio transceiver module provides the radio interface. Its battery supply powers the electronics, and its ground completes the electrical supply path needed for those electronics to operate.

sections.title: The sheet shows the vehicle-side interface
sections.body: The reference names the body control module, a K-LINE circuit, and medium-speed controller area network connections. These communication paths have different labels and should remain distinct when reading the illustration. Their presence explains why tire pressure information depends on more than the pressure-sensing devices at the wheels.

sections.title: Read supply, ground, and data separately
sections.body: The battery-voltage label identifies supply, the ground label identifies return, and the network plus and minus labels identify paired data paths. The always-live notation describes the marked supply. Connector and off-page references show how to continue tracing; the schematic does not depict the harness's physical route.

topics.title: Climate-controlled seat power and communication
topics.summary: This sheet shows the electrical supply and network connections associated with the front seat climate control module (SCME). Those paths let the module receive energy and exchange information for the seat's temperature-control functions.

sections.title: Power and messages perform different jobs
sections.body: Battery supply provides the energy needed by the module and its controlled functions, while ground completes the electrical return path. The medium-speed controller area network (MS-CAN) carries digital messages. Its paired communication wires convey information rather than acting as the main power supply for seat climate operation.

sections.title: The supply can remain available with ignition off
sections.body: The battery junction box (BJB), fuse F14 and “Hot at all times” label identify a protected battery supply on this sheet. That label describes voltage availability, not continuous heating or cooling. Module activity also depends on operating commands and conditions beyond the presence of battery power.

sections.title: Trace each type of connection separately
sections.body: Battery, ground and network labels provide useful starting points for reading the drawing. Connector, splice and ground identifiers let the path continue through other references. Follow the illustrated connections to establish the arrangement; this sheet's supply and communication labels do not by themselves describe the seat's complete internal heating or cooling hardware.

topics.title: Driver Seat Heating and Cooling Circuits
topics.summary: This sheet connects the left front seat’s cushion and backrest blower assemblies with the front seat climate-control module. It separates airflow control, temperature information and thermoelectric-device circuits within the climate-controlled seat system.

sections.title: Air movement and heat transfer work together
sections.body: The cushion and backrest each have a blower assembly that moves air through the seat. Thermoelectric devices transfer heat electrically, while temperature information lets the controller monitor conditions. These different jobs explain why each assembly has more wiring than a basic motor that only turns on and off.

sections.title: Why the diagram separates circuit families
sections.body: The labels distinguish blower control, sensor paths and thermoelectric device (TED) connections. Seat Control Module E (SCME), described here as the front seat climate-control module, links those functions. Separating the paths helps explain how airflow, temperature feedback and thermal output can be affected differently by a circuit concern.

sections.title: Following cushion and backrest connections
sections.body: The named cushion and backrest assemblies provide the clearest starting points for reading the sheet. Connector identifiers and the referenced splices carry their circuits through the harness to the module. Repeated wire labels identify continuing electrical paths; the drawing’s arrangement does not show the wires’ physical route inside the seat.

topics.title: Right Front Climate-Controlled Seat Wiring
topics.summary: This sheet connects the right-hand front seat’s cushion and backrest climate-control assemblies to their controller. It separates airflow control, thermoelectric operation, and temperature feedback.

sections.title: Airflow carries the heating or cooling effect
sections.body: The cushion and backrest each have a blower assembly. Air movement distributes the temperature effect through the seat, while a thermoelectric device (TED) changes temperature using electrical energy. Temperature-sensor connections provide feedback, allowing the controller to relate its commands to the conditions developing within each assembly.

sections.title: Why each assembly needs several circuits
sections.body: The front seat climate control module has separate connections for blower control, thermoelectric drive, and sensor information. These are different electrical jobs: moving air requires motor power, changing temperature requires device power, and measuring temperature requires a signal and reference path. Combining them in one assembly does not make their circuits interchangeable.

sections.title: Following cushion and backrest labels
sections.body: The repeated cushion and backrest label patterns help distinguish the two branches. Positive and negative drive labels belong to their respective loads, while sensor-return labels identify measurement paths. Connector and splice references show electrical continuity through the harness; the drawing does not describe the physical airflow passages inside the seat.

topics.title: Driver power-seat switch and motor circuits
topics.summary: Power-seat motors turn electrical energy into changes in seating position and support. This sheet includes the driver's seat arrangement labeled without memory, with adjustment-switch, motor, supply and ground references.

sections.title: Different motors produce different adjustments
sections.body: The track motor moves the seat forward or rearward, while height and tilt motors change its vertical position and cushion angle. The power-lumbar assembly changes lower-back support. These separate mechanisms explain why one adjustment can be affected while another remains available, even though both are operated from the seat-control switch.

sections.title: Direction depends on the electrical command
sections.body: Reversible seat motors move in opposite directions when the polarity across their drive connections reverses. The switch's fore, aft, up and down labels identify the requested movements. Following those labeled circuits helps relate a control action to the intended motor instead of treating every switch output as a common power feed.

sections.title: Reading the supply and equipment notes
sections.body: The battery junction box, fuse and ground references describe the available electrical supply. “Hot at all times” means power availability does not itself depend on the ignition being on. The without-memory annotation identifies the illustrated arrangement; connector identities and drawn paths establish its details rather than assumptions from a memory-seat system.

topics.title: Passenger Power Seat Motor Circuits
topics.summary: This power-seat sheet includes the passenger six-way adjustment circuit, with separate motors for fore-and-aft travel, height, and tilt. The electrical controls turn the occupant's directional request into movement of the seat mechanism.

sections.title: Separate motors create different adjustments
sections.body: The track motor moves the seat forward or rearward, while the height and tilt motors change its vertical position and angle. Reversing current through a conventional seat motor reverses its rotation. The switch's paired direction labels therefore describe opposite movements of a mechanism, rather than separate motors for every direction.

sections.title: Why the supply and grounds appear together
sections.body: The drawing identifies a fused battery-junction-box feed, ground references, the front seat control switch, and the motor connections. These provide the electrical context for powered movement. Comparing the named motor paths helps distinguish the circuit serving one adjustment from the supply arrangements used by the wider seat system.

sections.title: Keep equipment labels with their branches
sections.body: The passenger adjustment branch is labeled explicitly, and a climate-controlled-seats label also appears on the sheet. That label should be interpreted with its illustrated branch rather than applied to every motor circuit. Connector and continuation references establish electrical relationships; they do not show how the harness is physically routed under the seat.

topics.title: Passenger power seat movement
topics.summary: The power seat mechanism uses electric motors to change the seat’s position. This sheet includes the passenger seat adjustment switch and the motors responsible for horizontal movement, height and tilt.

sections.title: Motor rotation becomes seat movement
sections.body: Each motor drives a mechanism that changes one aspect of seat position. Horizontal movement shifts the seat forward or rearward, while height and tilt change the cushion’s elevation and angle. Reversing the electrical polarity across a conventional seat motor reverses its rotation and therefore the direction of adjustment.

sections.title: Separate a shared supply from individual adjustments
sections.body: The drawing names the right-hand front seat control switch, its adjustment motors, the battery junction box (BJB) and a ground reference. Seeing these together helps explain why a supply concern can affect several adjustments, while an individual motor circuit relates to a particular movement.

sections.title: Read each adjustment branch
sections.body: Use the horizontal, height and tilt labels to identify the relevant motor branch, then follow the illustrated switch contacts and wires. The passenger six-way seat label identifies the shown adjustment arrangement. A climate-controlled seats label also appears; its exact branch scope must come from the illustration, rather than being assumed for every circuit.

topics.title: Memory-seat selection wiring
topics.summary: Memory-seat controls let the driver select stored seating positions through electrical requests. This sheet focuses on the memory switch, driver door module, and the power and communication paths supporting those requests.

sections.title: A button sends a request
sections.body: The memory switch has separate selection circuits and a return path associated with the driver door module (DDM). These inputs identify the requested memory selection. They are different from the higher-current circuits that physically drive a seat motor, which are not established by this sheet’s switch labels.

sections.title: Why door controls share the reference
sections.body: The drawing also identifies the front-door lock switch and master window control, along with a protected battery junction box (BJB) supply and ground references. Showing these interfaces together helps explain the driver-door electronics involved. Loss of module power can affect more than one local control function.

sections.title: Read the page scope and local branches
sections.body: The MEMORY heading applies to the whole sheet. The medium-speed Controller Area Network pair carries module messages, and continuation references lead to window, lock and network information. The smaller coupe box is local to C535 on the master-window-switch return path. Keeping that local connector alternative separate from the page heading avoids treating the entire memory-seat switch arrangement as coupe-only.

topics.title: Memory seat power and communication
topics.summary: The driver seat module coordinates the electrical functions used by the memory seat system. This sheet focuses on the module's battery supplies, ground paths and vehicle-network connection, which support its ability to receive information and operate.

sections.title: Power and information reach the module
sections.body: The driver seat module (DSM) needs electrical supply for its circuitry and the functions it controls. It also connects to the medium-speed controller area network (MS-CAN), a paired-wire communication system. Network messages carry information between modules without requiring a separate wire for every individual message.

sections.title: Why the support circuits matter
sections.body: The drawing distinguishes power and logic grounds alongside battery-voltage inputs. These labels help separate the module's operating needs from its motor-output circuits shown elsewhere. Loss of supply, an impaired return path or disrupted communication can each affect module operation, so a seat concern alone does not identify which function is missing.

sections.title: Trace the labeled circuit roles
sections.body: The battery junction box (BJB), body control module (BCM), fuses and ground reference provide starting points for following the illustrated paths. Battery-voltage labels identify supply inputs, while the network plus and minus labels identify the communication pair. Continuation references lead to other sheets; they do not describe physical harness routing.

topics.title: Seat adjustment switches in the memory-seat system
topics.summary: This memory-seat sheet covers the driver's adjustment switch, driver seat module (DSM) and power lumbar assembly. It helps distinguish the driver's movement requests from the electrical paths serving the lumbar adjustment hardware.

sections.title: The switch describes the movement being requested
sections.body: Horizontal, height and tilt labels represent different directions of seat adjustment. The corresponding switch circuits let the DSM recognize a requested movement. Lumbar adjustment changes support against the occupant's lower back, and its inflate and deflate labels describe a separate support function from moving the seat frame.

sections.title: The sheet connects commands with their electrical support
sections.body: The battery junction box (BJB), fuse F12 and ground reference identify supply infrastructure alongside the adjustment circuits. A “Hot at all times” label means the indicated supply remains available independently of ignition position. It does not mean the seat or lumbar assembly should move continuously.

sections.title: Follow direction labels through the actual drawing
sections.body: The switch and module use matching movement descriptions that help orient a circuit trace. The lumbar assembly has its own labeled connections, and an alternative marked “or” requires attention to the illustrated branch. The sheet explains electrical relationships, not the physical route of wires inside the seat.

topics.title: Memory seat motors and feedback
topics.summary: The memory seat system moves the driver's seat electrically and tracks its movement so stored positions can be recalled. This sheet shows the driver seat module, the left-hand seat adjustment motors and their Hall-effect feedback circuits.

sections.title: Movement needs feedback
sections.body: The track motor moves the seat forward and backward, while the height and tilt motors change its vertical position and angle. Hall-effect sensing detects magnetic changes associated with motor movement. That feedback gives the driver seat module (DSM) information about movement as it controls the adjustments.

sections.title: Motor drive and sensing have different jobs
sections.body: A memory system needs both the ability to move the seat and information about that movement. Motor circuits carry the electrical drive, while the labeled sense and return circuits serve the feedback side. A movement concern therefore needs to be understood in terms of both functions before interpreting diagnostic results.

sections.title: Follow each adjustment through the drawing
sections.body: Use the track, height and tilt labels to identify the adjustment being discussed, then follow its drawn connections to the module. Forward, aft, up and down describe movement commands. Connector identifiers and location references help identify the hardware; the schematic itself describes electrical relationships rather than the wiring's physical route.

topics.title: Power mirrors without heat or memory
topics.summary: Power-mirror motors change the angle of the reflective glass so the driver can adjust the rearward view. This diagram applies to mirrors without heating or memory and shows their switch, motor, supply, and ground relationships.

sections.title: Reversing a motor changes direction
sections.body: Each mirror has motor functions for horizontal and vertical movement. The switch arrangement reverses electrical polarity to reverse a motor’s direction, allowing adjustment both ways along each axis. The direction labels in the drawing describe these movements rather than separate motors for every individual direction.

sections.title: How the driver’s control reaches both mirrors
sections.body: The exterior-mirror control is shown with the master window control switch assembly. Its circuits select the driver or passenger mirror and the desired movement. The supply comes through the body control module (BCM) accessory-delay arrangement, while the ground network completes the switch’s electrical connection.

sections.title: Following the applicable mirror circuit
sections.body: Motor symbols and polarity markings explain movement, while connector and splice references show the electrical path to each side. The G301 reference identifies the ground connection. The explicit 'without heated mirrors' and 'without memory' qualifiers are essential; this sheet does not describe heater operation or memory-position electronics.

topics.title: Heated power mirrors without memory
topics.summary: This sheet covers heated exterior mirrors without memory equipment. Small motors adjust the viewing angle of the glass, while separate connections support heating, turn signals, puddle lamps and the illustrated folding interface.

sections.title: Motor direction changes the view
sections.body: The mirror's adjustment motors move the glass along horizontal and vertical axes. Reversing the electrical drive changes the direction of movement. The exterior mirror switch selects the requested side and direction, while heating and lamp functions use their own circuits rather than performing the glass-adjustment work.

sections.title: One assembly contains several electrical functions
sections.body: A mirror can adjust normally while a lamp or heater has a separate concern. This drawing brings those functions together so their individual feeds, returns and cross-references can be understood. It also identifies the body control module (BCM) and accessory-delay relay within the illustrated power arrangement.

sections.title: Read the page scope and local branches
sections.body: The HEATED MIRRORS / WITHOUT MEMORY heading applies to the whole sheet. Left/right and up/down labels identify the adjustment-motor paths, while return and fold identify other control functions. The local power-folding continuation leads to sheet 124-3; it does not make folding universal across this arrangement. Heating, interior-lighting and turn-signal references continue their respective circuits elsewhere.

topics.title: Power-folding mirrors without memory
topics.summary: This sheet covers power-folding mirrors without memory equipment. Electric motors move the mirror housings inward or outward, while a folding relay switches their drive circuits.

sections.title: Electrical drive creates folding movement
sections.body: A folding motor converts electrical energy into movement at the mirror hinge. Reversing its electrical drive changes the direction of movement. The relay's inward and outward labels help explain that switching function, while the illustrated circuit establishes how the left-hand and right-hand mirror motors are served.

sections.title: Separating motor drive from its supply
sections.body: The body control module (BCM), fused supply and ground reference provide context for the folding circuit. A motor requires a complete current path to move, so the sheet helps separate the source of power, the switching arrangement and the conductors carrying that power to the mirror.

sections.title: Following the applicable mirror branch
sections.body: The “Power folding mirrors” and “Without memory” headings apply to this entire sheet. Use its connector identifiers and continuation to follow that arrangement into the related mirror circuit. The always-live annotation describes supply availability rather than a continuous folding command; memory-equipped arrangements require their own references.

topics.title: Memory Mirror Switch and Module Circuits
topics.summary: This power-mirror sheet shows the driver door module (DDM), its electrical support and the memory-set switch circuits. It helps explain how a driver’s preset selection reaches the electronics that coordinate memory-equipped mirror functions.

sections.title: A memory button supplies a request
sections.body: The memory-set switch provides separate preset-selection inputs and a return path. These circuits communicate the driver’s choice to the module rather than carrying mirror-motor operating current. The DDM also has a medium-speed controller area network connection, allowing information to be exchanged with other participating vehicle electronics.

sections.title: Why supply and ground appear with switch inputs
sections.body: The module needs its battery supply and ground to interpret switch activity and participate in network communication. The battery junction box and ground references identify those supporting paths. A supply concern can affect the module broadly, while an individual switch-input concern can affect only a particular request.

sections.title: Recognizing the memory-related portion
sections.body: The “Memory” heading applies to this whole module-and-switch arrangement. It does not make memory equipment universal across power mirrors. Follow the connector and continuation references to relate these preset inputs and module supplies to mirror operation on the other sheets, keeping switch requests distinct from motor-drive circuits.

topics.title: Memory mirror switch communication
topics.summary: This sheet covers the mirror-switch communication arrangement for vehicles with memory. It shows how the driver’s mirror-position requests relate to the driver door module and master-window controls, with coupe-specific switch connections marked separately.

sections.title: A position request becomes information
sections.body: The mirror switch has a local interconnect network (LIN) connection, indicating that information is exchanged over a communication circuit. Its supply and return support that electronic function. The driver door module (DDM) is also named on the sheet, linking the switch reference to the door’s control electronics.

sections.title: Why accessory power appears here
sections.body: The body control module (BCM), a protected feed and the accessory-delay relay are included in this reference. These labels help distinguish the availability of electrical power from a request to move the mirror. A switch can depend on both a valid supply path and successful communication for its request to be recognized.

sections.title: Reading the equipment branches
sections.body: “Memory” is the heading for the whole sheet. The coupe labels are narrower: they mark the C535 connections at the mirror switch, rather than defining every connection on the page. Follow those local markers and the continuation to the adjoining mirror sheet to trace the appropriate switch, master-window and door-module arrangement.

topics.title: Memory-equipped driver mirror motors and feedback
topics.summary: This memory-equipped driver-mirror sheet identifies adjustment motors, position feedback, heating and lighting around the driver door module and left exterior mirror. The whole drawing applies to that memory arrangement.

sections.title: Movement and position are separate signals
sections.body: Small motors tilt the mirror horizontally and vertically, changing the rearward view. Position potentiometers are variable electrical elements that report mirror position. Their feed, return, and signal paths let a controller distinguish where the mirror is from the command that tells a motor to move.

sections.title: Several features share the mirror assembly
sections.body: The driver door module connects to heating, a turn indicator and puddle lighting as well as the adjustment circuits. Heating clears moisture through electrical heat, while the lamps provide signaling or nearby illumination. The “Memory” heading qualifies this complete arrangement, including the position-feedback circuits that distinguish it from simpler mirror systems.

sections.title: Use the function labels to follow each path
sections.body: Motor direction labels describe movement commands, while potentiometer labels describe position feedback. Ground and interior-lamp references provide additional tracing points. Treat these as separate functions within a shared assembly, and use the drawn connections to establish relationships instead of assuming that adjacent extracted labels share a circuit.

topics.title: Passenger mirror motors and feedback
topics.summary: This power-mirror sheet shows the right-hand exterior mirror and passenger door module (PDM). It brings together adjustment motors, position feedback and the mirror’s labeled heating and lighting functions.

sections.title: Movement and position are different signals
sections.body: The mirror’s motors move the glass horizontally and vertically. Position potentiometers provide electrical feedback about the glass position, which is useful for memory operation. The potentiometer feed and return support that sensing function, while motor circuits provide the drive that actually changes where the glass points.

sections.title: Several functions share the mirror housing
sections.body: The sheet also names passenger mirror heating, turn indication and puddle lighting. These are separate functions despite sharing one mirror assembly. The memory annotation identifies the relevant illustrated circuitry; it should not be used to assume that every Mustang mirror has position feedback or the same set of lamps.

sections.title: Separating motor, sensor and lamp paths
sections.body: Read the function labels beside the PDM and mirror together with the drawn conductors. The interior-lamp continuation helps follow the lighting portion, while ground and splice identifiers provide circuit landmarks. A shared connector does not make all mirror functions one circuit, and nearby text does not establish a shared electrical path.

topics.title: Interior auto-dimming mirror circuits
topics.summary: An auto-dimming interior mirror reduces reflected glare by changing the reflectivity of its glass. This power-mirror sheet identifies the mirror’s power, ground and reverse-related electrical interfaces.

sections.title: Electrical control changes the reflection
sections.body: Auto-dimming mirrors use an electrically controlled layer in the glass to reduce glare from lights behind the vehicle. Their electronics need a supply and return path to make that change. A reverse input provides operating context, although the exact response to that input belongs to the system’s operation reference.

sections.title: Why reverse and accessory labels appear
sections.body: The sheet names the body control module (BCM), accessory delay relay and reverse-lamp field-effect transistor (FET) output alongside the mirror. Those labels help distinguish electrical supply control from reverse-state information. The rain-sensitive-wiper label marks equipment context within the drawing and does not make every circuit exclusive to that option.

sections.title: Trace supply, return and information separately
sections.body: At the mirror, the supply, reverse and ground labels describe different electrical jobs. The always-live supply notes describe availability upstream, not continuous operation of every device. Connector, splice and ground references support circuit tracing; the illustrated lines establish the paths, while the schematic does not show physical harness routing.

topics.title: Audio display power and signals
topics.summary: The front control/display interface module (FCDIM) provides an electronic display interface within the audio and navigation system. This sheet identifies its power, ground, communication, and rear-video connections.

sections.title: Different paths support different functions
sections.body: The display needs electrical power to operate, data to coordinate with other modules, and a video signal for the pictured rear-video function. A fault in one category can affect a different part of its behavior. The video pair and network pair therefore need to be understood as distinct interfaces.

sections.title: Why the supply appears beside network wiring
sections.body: The page identifies a fused supply associated with the body control module (BCM), a ground reference, and a source labeled hot at all times. That supply availability is different from a command to display information. The high-speed Controller Area Network 3 (HS3 CAN) pair supports electronic message exchange.

sections.title: Following the continuation labels
sections.body: Parking-aid and module-network references indicate where related information continues. Their placement in extracted text does not establish the exact electrical connection; the drawn lines do that. The coupe label qualifies illustrated content, so its scope must be read on the diagram rather than applied automatically to the entire audio system.

topics.title: Radio power, data and antenna circuits
topics.summary: This audio-system sheet brings together the radio’s supply, communication and antenna connections. It distinguishes the audio control module (ACM), antenna equipment and vehicle-control references that support radio operation.

sections.title: Reception and control use different paths
sections.body: An antenna captures radio signals, and an antenna amplifier strengthens received signals where fitted. Coaxial cable carries radio-frequency information with shielding that reduces interference. The high-speed controller area network (CAN) pair carries module messages instead, while battery supply and ground provide operating energy to the electronics.

sections.title: Why the sheet includes starting and body circuits
sections.body: The drawing names the starter relay, powertrain control module and body control module alongside the ACM. Start-related information and power references help place radio operation in the vehicle’s wider electrical context. The antenna power labels also distinguish an amplifier’s electrical supply from the received signal carried by its coaxial connection.

sections.title: Recognizing antenna variants
sections.body: The sheet includes a coupe on-glass antenna label, a convertible branch and satellite-radio antenna references. These labels describe applicable illustrated branches, rather than making every antenna universal. Connector identities, shielding symbols and continuation references establish each path; engine labels elsewhere on the drawing do not define the whole sheet’s applicability.

topics.title: Audio speaker circuits
topics.summary: This sheet follows the audio control module (ACM) and the speaker circuits used to turn electrical audio signals into sound. It identifies front door woofers, pillar tweeters and rear speakers so each channel can be followed through the reference.

sections.title: How electrical signals become sound
sections.body: A speaker’s moving coil responds to a changing electrical signal, moving its diaphragm and the surrounding air. Woofers reproduce lower frequencies, while tweeters reproduce higher frequencies. The left and right channels preserve the placement of sounds, making correct channel identification important when interpreting the diagram.

sections.title: Why the channel pairs matter
sections.body: The sheet labels left-front, right-front, left-rear and right-rear speaker outputs with positive and negative designations. Those markings describe each audio pair’s polarity; a negative speaker connection is not automatically a body ground. Maintaining the intended relationship between paired wires matters because reversed speaker motion can change how sounds combine.

sections.title: Following the illustrated branches
sections.body: Connector and splice labels let you follow the drawn paths between the module and speakers. Coupe and convertible labels identify branches that need to be matched to the vehicle. Their presence does not make every speaker connection identical across body styles, and adjacent extracted labels do not establish a connection.

topics.title: 2.3L active noise-control microphones
topics.summary: This 2.3L sheet shows microphones that measure cabin sound for active noise control and their paired connections to the audio control module. The drawing separates coupe and convertible rear-microphone arrangements.

sections.title: Using sound to reduce sound
sections.body: Microphones convert pressure changes in the air into electrical signals. An active noise-control system uses those signals to generate sound that opposes selected unwanted noise. The timing matters: properly opposed sound reduces the resulting pressure variation, while the microphones provide feedback about what is happening inside the cabin.

sections.title: Why several microphone identities appear
sections.body: The sheet names front, rear, left-rear and right-rear active noise-control microphones. Multiple sensing positions let the system receive information from different cabin areas. Their ambient-noise channel labels keep those inputs distinct, helping the reader follow the correct microphone circuit into the audio control module.

sections.title: Recognizing signal pairs and variants
sections.body: The 2.3L heading applies to the complete sheet. A convertible box contains the left-rear and right-rear microphones, while the coupe box contains the single rear microphone; the front microphone is outside those boxes. Positive and negative ambient-noise labels identify paired microphone signals, not speaker outputs.

topics.title: SYNC and Positioning Module Wiring
topics.summary: This audio-navigation sheet shows power, ground and network connections for the SYNC module and Global Positioning System Module (GPSM). It explains how these units receive electrical supply and exchange information with the vehicle.

sections.title: Multimedia and position information
sections.body: The GPSM supplies positioning information, while the SYNC module, also identified as the Accessory Protocol Interface Module (APIM), supports the multimedia interface. The sheet focuses on the connections that let these units operate and communicate. It does not show speaker outputs or the complete navigation signal chain.

sections.title: Supply paths differ from message paths
sections.body: Battery-voltage and ground labels describe the operating supply, with the Body Control Module (BCM) and fuse reference shown upstream. The 'Hot at all times' notation describes supply availability. Medium-speed and high-speed Controller Area Network (CAN) pairs carry messages separately from the wires supplying electrical energy.

sections.title: Follow the named network branch
sections.body: The distinct CAN labels identify different communication branches, while connector, splice and ground references help trace their relationships. The coupe notation is an applicability cue attached to the illustrated wiring and should remain with that detail. Continuation references extend the electrical diagram; they do not indicate physical harness routing.

topics.title: Microphone and audio input signal wiring
topics.summary: This sheet identifies audio signal circuits associated with the overhead console, audio input socket, SYNC module, and audio control module. These paths carry microphone and entertainment audio information between the relevant components.

sections.title: Where the sound information begins
sections.body: The overhead-console microphone converts speech into an electrical signal, while the audio input socket accepts sound from an external source. The SYNC accessory protocol interface module (APIM) handles connected functions, and the audio control module (ACM) handles audio-system operation. Their labels establish the components involved without defining every connection.

sections.title: Why signal pairs and shields matter
sections.body: Left and right stereo channels preserve separate sound information, while mono labels identify a single audio channel. Positive and negative labels distinguish signal conductors. Shields reduce unwanted electrical interference reaching sensitive audio paths; a shield label does not make that conductor interchangeable with an audio signal return.

sections.title: Following a particular audio path
sections.body: Microphone, stereo input, stereo output, and shield labels describe different functions even when their wires share a connector. Circuit identifiers and wire colors help follow each function through the illustrated reference. Actual line connections establish the path; neighboring labels in extracted text do not establish that two terminals are connected.

topics.title: Steering-Column Module Power and Data
topics.summary: This audio-system sheet shows the steering column control module (SCCM) with its power, ground and communication connections. Those connections let a steering-column electronic controller operate and exchange information with the wider vehicle network.

sections.title: Why an audio reference includes this module
sections.body: Modern controls can communicate requests electronically instead of using a separate wire for every function. The SCCM is a steering-column controller, and its network connection gives other modules access to information it handles. On this sheet, the emphasis is its electrical support and data path rather than speaker wiring.

sections.title: Supply and communication are separate
sections.body: The battery-voltage label marks the operating supply, and the ground label marks its return. The high-speed Controller Area Network (CAN) pair carries messages. The body control module (BCM), fuse, ground and splice references provide context for tracing these paths, while the always-live label describes the marked supply’s availability.

sections.title: Following the sheet into other references
sections.body: Connector labels identify the SCCM interface, while network and power-distribution references continue the explanation on other sheets. A network pair does not carry speaker-level audio merely because it appears in an audio section. The illustrated lines establish connections; label order in extracted text does not establish topology or physical routing.

topics.title: Steering-wheel audio and menu switch wiring
topics.summary: The upper steering-wheel switches provide menu and audio commands without requiring the driver to reach the center controls. This sheet shows their relationship with the clockspring and steering column control module (SCCM).

sections.title: Commands cross a rotating connection
sections.body: The clockspring contains flexible conductors arranged to maintain electrical continuity as the steering wheel turns. This lets wheel-mounted switches remain connected to stationary vehicle wiring. The SCCM receives switch information, while the labeled illumination circuits serve the separate purpose of making the controls visible in low light.

sections.title: Different switch groups share the steering wheel
sections.body: The left upper group includes directional and confirmation commands, while the right upper group includes volume and other audio-related labels. Their signals need to remain distinguishable even though the controls are physically close. This sheet helps identify the relevant group and its electrical path through the rotating interface.

sections.title: Distinguish sensing returns from illumination
sections.body: Analog-to-digital (A/D) channel and return labels identify how switch inputs are presented to the electronics. They should be read separately from panel-illumination references and the named ground. Follow the drawn connections through the clockspring symbols; label proximity alone does not establish which switch uses a particular channel.

topics.title: Steering-wheel phone and voice controls
topics.summary: This audio-system sheet follows the lower right-hand steering-wheel switch functions for phone, mute and voice control. It shows how their electrical paths relate to the clockspring and steering column control module (SCCM).

sections.title: A rotating wheel needs a flexible connection
sections.body: The clockspring uses a coiled flexible electrical connection to accommodate steering-wheel rotation while maintaining circuits to the stationary column wiring. The switch pack provides driver inputs rather than carrying speaker output. The SCCM’s analog-to-digital (A/D) channels allow electrical input levels to be interpreted by its electronics.

sections.title: Shared hardware appears in several systems
sections.body: The sheet names phone controls, mute and voice alongside references to cruise control and cluster-and-panel illumination. These references reflect other functions using the steering-wheel and column wiring area. They do not mean every named function shares the same conductor or that this sheet contains the complete audio system.

sections.title: Separate input channels, returns and cross-references
sections.body: The A/D channel labels identify input interfaces, and the return label identifies their associated electrical reference. Connector and ground identifiers support tracing through the illustrated clockspring paths. Continuation references lead to related circuits; their physical placement in extracted text cannot substitute for the drawing’s connection lines.

topics.title: Front controls module power and communication
topics.summary: The front controls interface module provides an electronic interface for the vehicle's front-panel controls. This audio-system sheet identifies its battery supply, ground and network communication connection.

sections.title: Controls need a communication path
sections.body: The front controls interface module, abbreviated FCIM, turns control activity into information the vehicle's electronics can use. Its role differs from that of a speaker or display. The power connection lets its electronics operate, while the network connection allows control information to reach other participating modules.

sections.title: The paired wires carry messages
sections.body: The Medium-Speed Controller Area Network, or MS-CAN, uses a pair of data conductors. The plus and minus labels identify the communication pair rather than a power feed and chassis return. The separate ground connection provides the module's electrical return, so data wiring and operating-power wiring need to be read as distinct functions.

sections.title: Understanding the supply and continuation labels
sections.body: The body control module and fuse reference identify the illustrated supply context. “Hot at all times” means that the feed remains available with the ignition off; it does not mean the controls are always actively operating. Network continuation references connect this page to communications information rather than describing physical wire routing.

topics.title: Audio Power, Antennas and Network Links
topics.summary: This audio-system sheet connects the audio control module (ACM) with its power, ground, antenna and communication paths. It helps explain how broadcast signals reach the radio while vehicle electrical information reaches the same unit through other circuits.

sections.title: Radio signals and vehicle messages differ
sections.body: Coaxial cables carry weak antenna signals within a shield that limits unwanted interference. Separate wires provide electrical power and ground. The high-speed controller area network (HS-CAN) connection carries vehicle messages, while the amplitude-modulation and frequency-modulation (AM/FM) antenna paths carry the broadcasts the radio receives.

sections.title: Several supporting systems appear together
sections.body: The sheet includes the battery junction box, antenna amplifier, body and powertrain control modules, and a starter-related branch. It also identifies a global positioning system (GPS) and satellite digital audio radio service (SDARS) antenna. These connections explain why radio reception, electrical supply and vehicle-state information require different tracing paths.

sections.title: Follow body-style and branch labels
sections.body: The coupe's on-glass antenna and the convertible arrangement are explicitly distinguished. Engine labels near the starting circuitry qualify those branches rather than the whole audio system. Ground, shield, switched-supply and always-powered labels describe electrical function; connector references and continuation markers lead to supporting sheets, not physical cable routes.

topics.title: Audio processing module power and data
topics.summary: The audio digital signal processing (DSP) module shapes audio signals within the sound system. This diagram shows the electrical supply, ground, and network connections that support its operation.

sections.title: Processing sound needs power and information
sections.body: Digital audio processing can alter characteristics such as frequency balance before sound reaches the speakers. The module needs electrical power to perform that work and communication paths to exchange operating information. The paired network wires shown here carry data; they are separate from the module’s battery supply and ground.

sections.title: Why this sheet separates support circuits
sections.body: The drawing identifies a fused feed associated with the body control module (BCM), a G201 ground connection, and high-speed controller area network 3 (HS3 CAN) connections. Separating these roles helps explain how a module can have a supply concern, a return-path concern, or a communication concern.

sections.title: Reading battery and network labels
sections.body: VBATT denotes battery voltage, GND denotes ground, and the CAN plus and minus labels identify the paired communication circuits. 'Hot at all times' describes the feed’s availability, rather than continuous audio playback. Connector and page references continue the electrical trace without specifying the module’s physical harness route.

topics.title: Audio signals between control modules
topics.summary: The audio control module (ACM) and audio digital signal processing (DSP) module exchange signals used to produce cabin sound. This diagram separates music, warning chimes, sound-management channels and the audio-enable circuit.

sections.title: Different sounds use identifiable paths
sections.body: Left and right audio channels carry program sound, while separately labeled chime channels carry warning sounds. The drawing also identifies active noise cancellation (ANC) and engine sound enhancement (ESE) channels. Those labels describe specialized sound functions; their presence does not establish that every Mustang has each feature.

sections.title: Signal pairs preserve useful information
sections.body: The positive and negative labels identify paired signal conductors. Such pairs let receiving electronics interpret the signal difference while reducing sensitivity to interference shared by both wires. Shield labels identify another means of limiting unwanted electrical noise. A signal's negative conductor should not automatically be read as an ordinary body ground.

sections.title: Use input and output labels as guides
sections.body: The OUT and IN descriptions help identify the sending and receiving ends of corresponding functions. Audio enable is a control path, distinct from the changing waveforms that represent sound. Follow the actual drawn connections and connector references to establish channel pairing; adjacent labels in extracted text do not establish a connection.

topics.title: Audio module and speaker circuits
topics.summary: This audio-system sheet identifies the digital signal processing (DSP) module and speaker circuits used in the touchscreen audio reference. The speakers turn electrical audio signals into sound, with different speaker types handling different portions of that sound.

sections.title: Different speakers reproduce different frequencies
sections.body: A speaker's moving element responds to a changing electrical signal and pushes air to create sound. Tweeters reproduce higher frequencies, while woofers and midwoofers handle lower ranges. This sheet names pillar tweeters, front-door speakers, rear speakers and an instrument-panel speaker alongside the audio DSP module.

sections.title: Keep each audio channel identifiable
sections.body: Speaker circuits are labeled by position and by positive and negative connection. That pairing preserves the intended polarity of cone movement between speakers; reversing a connection can change how their sound combines. A speaker-negative label identifies part of its audio circuit and should not be treated as a generic body ground.

sections.title: Follow the appropriate body-style branch
sections.body: Coupe and convertible labels appear within the speaker reference and qualify the illustrated branches where shown. Connector identifiers, circuit names and splice references establish the actual paths. The schematic explains electrical relationships, while its location references help find components; speaker names arranged near one another do not establish a shared connection.

topics.title: Rear Subwoofer and Amplifier Wiring
topics.summary: The rear subwoofer produces low-frequency sound using power from its own amplifier. This sheet separates the audio signal, amplifier enable command, electrical supply, and speaker output.

sections.title: A small audio signal controls larger speaker current
sections.body: The digital signal processing (DSP) module sends the subwoofer audio signal to the rear amplifier. The amplifier uses its battery supply to produce the current needed to move the subwoofer cone. Its enable connection has a separate role: it controls amplifier operation rather than carrying the bass audio itself.

sections.title: Why power and shielding are shown separately
sections.body: The diagram includes a fused supply from the body control module (BCM), a ground connection, and shielding associated with the audio wiring. Shielding reduces unwanted electrical interference in the signal path. An always-live supply can be available while the amplifier remains inactive because supply availability and the enable command are separate conditions.

sections.title: Following the signal through the amplifier
sections.body: Read the positive and negative subwoofer labels in relation to the component boundary: the amplifier has an incoming audio pair and an outgoing speaker pair. Those labels do not make every negative audio conductor a chassis ground. Connector and ground references help distinguish signal continuity from the amplifier’s power circuit.

topics.title: 2.3L active noise-control microphone circuits
topics.summary: This 2.3L audio-system sheet shows the microphones used to observe cabin sound for active noise control. It distinguishes coupe and convertible rear-microphone arrangements while identifying the front microphone and their audio control module connections.

sections.title: Cabin sound becomes a control signal
sections.body: A microphone converts changing air pressure into an electrical waveform. Active noise-control electronics use those observations to shape sound intended to reduce selected unwanted noise. The microphones on this sheet therefore observe the cabin sound field; their purpose differs from sending a driver’s voice to a phone call.

sections.title: Microphone arrangements vary by configuration
sections.body: “2.3L” is the heading for the whole sheet. The convertible dashed box contains left-rear and right-rear microphones; the separate coupe box contains the rear microphone. The front microphone is drawn outside those body-style boxes. These alternatives should not be combined into a claim that every listed rear microphone is installed together.

sections.title: Follow each paired signal to its reference
sections.body: The audio control module (ACM) entries identify ambient-noise channels with positive and negative signal paths. Inline connector references show harness interfaces along the illustrated routes. Trace the matching configuration through those lines; wire-color changes and adjacent labels in extracted text do not establish channel identity or an electrical junction.

topics.title: Navigation and SYNC electrical paths
topics.summary: This sheet identifies power, ground, communication and video connections associated with navigation and SYNC equipment. It shows the global positioning system module (GPSM), the accessory protocol interface module (APIM) used by SYNC and related body-control references.

sections.title: Position information and display functions
sections.body: The GPSM supplies positioning information, while the APIM supports SYNC functions and its display interface. Each requires electrical power and a ground return to operate. Data connections carry information between electronics, while the separately labeled video pair carries an image signal rather than an ordinary power feed.

sections.title: Separating several kinds of connection
sections.body: Medium-speed and high-speed controller area network (CAN) labels identify communication circuits on this sheet. The body control module (BCM), fuse reference and parking-aid continuation also appear. These references help relate a navigation or display concern to its electrical dependencies without treating every wire as the same type of signal.

sections.title: Following pairs and continuation references
sections.body: The plus and minus CAN labels identify paired data conductors, not ordinary positive power and chassis ground. Battery-voltage and ground labels identify those separate functions. The illustrated lines establish which module uses each path; continuation references lead to the network and parking-aid sheets without describing physical cable routing.

topics.title: SYNC microphone and audio paths
topics.summary: This touchscreen audio-system sheet shows signal interfaces between the overhead microphone, SYNC module, and audio control module (ACM). These paths carry voice input and audio information between components with different jobs.

sections.title: Voice input and sound output
sections.body: The microphone converts sound into an electrical signal for the SYNC accessory protocol interface module (APIM). The sheet also identifies stereo and mono interfaces between that module and the ACM. Separating incoming voice from outgoing audio helps explain how a voice feature can involve several components rather than a single radio assembly.

sections.title: Protecting small audio signals
sections.body: Microphone and audio signals can be affected by unwanted electrical interference. Shield labels identify protection associated with these signal circuits, while positive and negative labels identify paired conductors. A shield has a different role from the wanted audio signal, so those paths should remain distinct when interpreting the drawing.

sections.title: Reading input and output labels
sections.body: An input or output label is written from the perspective of the component beside it. Follow the illustrated line to understand the corresponding interface at the other component. Connector references and continuation markers maintain circuit identity; the diagram describes electrical relationships rather than the physical routing between console and dashboard.

topics.title: Media-hub and SYNC signal wiring
topics.summary: The media hub provides connections for external audio and digital devices in the touchscreen entertainment system. This sheet identifies its audio, power, ground, shielding and digital-cable relationships with the SYNC module.

sections.title: Analog sound and digital information take different paths
sections.body: Auxiliary left and right audio channels carry changing electrical signals representing sound. Universal Serial Bus (USB) carries digital information through its designated cable. The SYNC module, identified as the accessory protocol interface module (APIM), interfaces with these media connections so external content can enter the entertainment system.

sections.title: Why power, return and shielding are separate
sections.body: The hub needs electrical power, while its media ground provides a return reference. Shielding reduces unwanted electrical interference reaching sensitive signal paths. These jobs differ from the positive and negative sides of the audio channels, which should be understood as paired signal connections rather than assumed battery and ground terminals.

sections.title: Following each named media function
sections.body: The repeated left, right, power, media-ground and shield labels help identify corresponding functions at the illustrated components. Connector callouts and the separately drawn USB cable establish the reference points. The diagram describes electrical relationships; it does not show the cable’s physical route or prove that a media problem originates in the hub.

topics.title: Steering-column power and audio-system networking
topics.summary: This audio-system wiring sheet shows the steering column control module (SCCM) with its electrical supply, ground, and communication circuits. These connections let the controller operate and exchange information with other vehicle electronics.

sections.title: Why a steering controller appears here
sections.body: The steering column controller handles inputs associated with steering-column controls. Information from a control can travel as a network message rather than as a separate wire running to every receiving device. Its appearance in the audio reference therefore highlights the electrical support and communication needed for coordinated control.

sections.title: Separating energy from information
sections.body: The battery-voltage and ground labels describe the controller's operating power paths. The paired high-speed Controller Area Network (CAN) labels identify communication conductors. A controller needs both usable power and communication to participate normally, so the network wires and supply wires answer different questions when reading this sheet.

sections.title: Following the supporting references
sections.body: The body control module (BCM), fuse, splice, and ground references provide connections to the wider electrical documentation. The hot-at-all-times label describes supply availability, not whether a feature is active. Follow the illustrated lines and continuation references for actual relationships; the drawing does not show physical harness routing.

topics.title: Steering-wheel audio and menu inputs
topics.summary: The upper steering-wheel switches provide menu-selection and audio-control inputs without requiring the driver to reach the center controls. This sheet shows their electrical paths through the clockspring to the steering-column controller.

sections.title: Button presses become electrical inputs
sections.body: The left upper group contains directional and confirmation controls, while the right upper group includes volume and other selection buttons. Their circuits lead to the Steering Column Control Module (SCCM). The module interprets switch inputs so the requested action can be handled by the relevant vehicle electronics.

sections.title: The wheel must remain connected while turning
sections.body: The clockspring provides a flexible electrical connection between the rotating steering wheel and fixed column. This sheet includes that transition because the switch path passes through it. It also references cluster and panel illumination, showing that button lighting and button-command circuits are related parts of the wheel assembly with different jobs.

sections.title: Keep input and illumination paths distinct
sections.body: Analog-to-digital (A/D) labels identify an input channel and associated returns used by the column electronics. The ground reference and illumination references lead to supporting circuit information. Trace each named switch group separately: sharing a clockspring or ground area does not make the left and right buttons the same electrical input.

topics.title: Steering-wheel phone and voice controls
topics.summary: The lower right-hand steering-wheel switch provides phone, mute and voice-command inputs. This diagram shows those controls alongside the clockspring and steering column control module (SCCM), which handles steering-column electrical inputs.

sections.title: Button presses become electrical inputs
sections.body: A button press changes a switch input that electronics can interpret as a requested function. The analog-to-digital (A/D) channel labels identify inputs whose electrical levels are read by the SCCM. These are control signals, so the steering-wheel buttons do not carry the audio power that ultimately drives the speakers.

sections.title: Connections must tolerate steering movement
sections.body: The clockspring maintains electrical connections between the rotating steering wheel and the stationary column using a flexible internal conductor arrangement. That lets the driver turn the wheel while retaining switch functions. Its appearance on this sheet explains an important part of the signal path between wheel-mounted controls and column electronics.

sections.title: Separate the neighboring steering-wheel functions
sections.body: The phone, mute and voice labels identify the functions of this switch, while cruise-control and illumination references connect the drawing to related sheets.
